9 Best Coffee Subscriptions, Reviewed & Reordered (2026)

📅 23 Sep 2021 | ⏱️ 35 min read (7038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~35 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, there’s nothing worse than dragging myself out of bed only to realize I’ve run out of coffee beans.
  • According to recent reports, whether you’re a third-wave coffee nerd looking to try a newly introduced craft roaster or a decaf drinker on the hunt for some actually good decaffeinated beans, there’s a subscription for you.
  • I know coffee preferences can be wide-ranging, which is why my team and I have scoured the earth for subscriptions that offer tailored picks for different kinds of coffee lovers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there’s nothing worse than dragging myself out of bed only to realize I’ve run out of coffee beans. That’s where coffee subscriptions come in. But the best services will do more than guarantee you’ll have a consistent supply of freshly roasted coffee—they also let you explore the vast world of coffee. They’re how I’ve discovered some of my favorite roasters, tried single-origins I never would have found on my own, and figured out exactly what I like and don’t like in a cup.

According to recent reports, whether you’re a third-wave coffee nerd looking to try a newly introduced craft roaster or a decaf drinker on the hunt for some actually good decaffeinated beans, there’s a subscription for you. After five years of testing, Trade is our top pick—but depending on what kind of coffee you like, I have plenty of other recommendations.

I know coffee preferences can be wide-ranging, which is why my team and I have scoured the earth for subscriptions that offer tailored picks for different kinds of coffee lovers. To date, we’ve tested nearly two dozen options and recommend the following wholeheartedly.

Newly introduced in this update: BA editors have been trying out some new deliveries, including some we’re loving from Methodical in Greenville, SC, and Fellow’s Drops program.

In a recent development, trade is a multi-roaster subscription that sources coffee from independent roasters all over the country. It's great for someone looking for great specialty coffee with an interest in trying a number of different roasters and different roasting styles.

Tester: Chris Morocco, food director This was the easiest subscription I have ever set up, and Trade did such a good job of hitting my preferences right in their sweet spot: medium roast, medium body, medium fruit…just medium all around. I have gotten stuck in the past, tasting the same coffees or coffee styles over and over, and after just two bags, I could tell this would be different.

It has been revealed that I set up an order for one 12-oz. bag of whole beans every two weeks. The first bag was Atomic Roasters Space Cadet out of Peabody, MA, and my second bag was Sparrows Coffee, Harmony Series All Seasons Blend from Grand Rapids, MI. I loved the Sparrows bag because it had just enough roast to feel pleasantly dense and weighty on my palate, yet with enough fruit, brightness, and acid to feel lively. When I clicked the box for “medium roast” coffee, this is exactly what I had in mind. I only do pour-over at home, and this was awesome in my Hario V60 coffee dripper.

Sources indicate that recently, senior shopping editor Olivia Tarantino tried Rarities, Trade’s newest program. It’s invite-only, with a rotating lineup of coffees that roasters make as experiments or passion projects. Each coffee is roasted and shipped to order, in batches of a few hundred bags at most. Trade provides detailed instructions direct from the roaster about how to best prepare your beans to get the optimal flavor extraction. She enjoyed an extended fermentation Chiroso variety that had complex acidity of citrus fruits and a slight savory flavor. We haven’t seen anything like Rarities from a subscription service, so serious coffee drinkers should jump on it.

The bottom line: There is a lot of great coffee in the world, but finding it and getting it right when you want it can be a challenge. Trade takes care of that for you, making this subscription absolutely worth it.

If you’re the kind of person who’s always ordering the fun new seasonal pour-over option at your local craft coffee shop, or who hunts down rare bean varietals like it’s your job, Podium Coffee Club’s Podium Platinum is the coffee subscription for you. Founded in 2023, Podium is a relatively new kid on the block in the world of coffee subs. The concept? A subscription service that solely sends out coffees that have stood on the podium (hence the name) at a major US coffee competition. The brand’s Podium Platinum subscription focuses on coffees that are unique and experimental in some way, be it flavor-wise, varietal-wise, or through the processing technique used.

Recent findings suggest that testers: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor, and Alaina Chou, commerce writer In the two months we’ve tested this service, we’ve received two bags of coffee that have lived up to that claim. The first bag was a light roast from Royal Flamingo Coffee, a micro-roaster based in Columbus, Ohio. The beans, grown in Colombia, were made using the Black Honey process and mossto lactic fermentation, which you can read more about on Podium’s website. The notes of blueberries, white chocolate, and florals definitely came through in the brewed coffee in both smell and taste, though not too aggressively. We quite enjoyed this one.

In a recent development, the next coffee hailed from Wonderstate Coffee in Wisconsin and claimed notes of gummy bear, melon, and cooked berries. That might seem like a crazy flavor profile for a bag of coffee, but the brewed stuff was subtle and highly drinkable.

The bottom line: This is a great coffee subscription to get if you’re looking to explore, nerd out on coffee-making processes, or discover award-winning roasters from across the country. Note that Podium also offers a less expensive Podium Gold subscription option, which does not get you the same unique selection that the Platinum offers.

In a recent development, if you’re a curious coffee connoisseur looking to try single-origin coffee from around the world while directly supporting fair trade and sustainable practices, Atlas is the subscription service for you. Every month, you’ll get a bag of single-origin coffee from a different country that comes with an ID card detailing sourcing information and tasting notes.

Tester: Kelly Janke, former director of culinary production The ordering process was easy. It asked me a few questions about my preferences in roast level, brewing type, and coffee quantity, with options ranging from a half bag to four bags per month. The shipping did seem to take longer than I expected, which was my main qualm with the service.

Sources indicate that the beans I received in my first month were medium roast from Rwanda. I really enjoyed the cards that came in the box with tasting notes and information on the growing region. I had chosen two bags per month because I drink a fair amount of coffee, but it’s worth noting that this meant I received two of the same exact coffee (which wasn’t clear at the time of ordering—I had assumed they would be different). I ground the beans in my Oxo burr coffee grinder to a medium grind and brewed them in a Chemex with a metal reusable filter using a 1:16 coffee-to-water ratio. The coffee definitely tasted on the darker side of a medium with notes of grape, red apple, and roasted almonds.

The bottom line: I love to try new coffee varieties and appreciate the difference; if you feel similarly, then Atlas is a great option for you.

According to recent reports, if you’ve been reading all of this as a decaf drinker, we have good news for you: there are also some great decaf coffee subscriptions out there, including Swiss Water. This subscription offers a rotating selection of decaf coffees from roasters all across the US, all of which have gone through the Swiss Water process, a chemical-free decaffeination technique that you can read more about here. Note that Swiss Water right now only offers whole bean coffees, so you’ll need to grind your own beans if you decide to try it out.

In a recent development, tester: Alaina Chou I opted for biweekly shipments, though Swiss Water also offers weekly, monthly, and bimonthly. The first coffee I received was from Manzanita Roasting Organization, based in San Diego. There was no informational card included, so all I really gathered about the coffee was that it was from Guatemala and had notes of berries and chocolate, which it did. For a decaf brew, I was impressed by the quality and nuance of the flavor. The same can be said for the second bag of beans I received, which was a blend called Kick Back from South Carolina–based Barista Alley.

The bottom line: You won’t find the kind of customization and curation options here that you see in most of the other subscriptions on this list, but if you’re okay with trying out a range of decaf coffees and aren’t married to one particular roast level or flavor profile, this service will work for you.

Of every coffee subscription we’ve ever tried, this one is unique. Most coffee beans, even if freshly roasted, are stored as green beans for months. Origin Roasted beans hit the roaster almost immediately after harvest and get shipped out right after that. Truly, they are the freshest coffee beans you can get without picking them yourself. It’s a subjective call as to whether that makes the flavor "better," but it makes it different.

According to recent reports, tester: Noah Kaufman Fruity or chocolate tasting notes that are present in beans that sit green are massively accentuated with Origin Roasted beans. If a flavorful cup of coffee is what you’re after, these beans are as flavorful as they come. The brand’s commitment to roasting at the beans’ origin has the added effect of bringing more coffee roasting work and expertise to countries of origin; roasting for most American coffees happens in the United States.

The ordering process is straightforward because there are no choices for you to make. Just give them your address and credit card number, and the coffee will be on its way to you at the end of each month. The firm only sends the beans it is harvesting that month, which come from a single farm somewhere in Central or South America. The locations are limited to ensure that Origin Roasted can actually get the beans to your door while they’re as fresh as they’re supposed to be.

Sources indicate that I got beans from all over Central and South America: Guatemala, Nicaragua, Panama, Colombia, Peru, and Brazil. Each coffee was entirely unlike the one that came before it. Shipments only get sent out on the 28th of every month, so I was limited to one bag per month.

According to recent reports, the bottom line: Because of the harvest and roast process, this really is a boutique product, so you can’t order en masse the way you can with larger roasters. I don’t think it makes sense to identify my favorite beans here because you, dear reader, are not guaranteed to get them anyway. What you are guaranteed to get are incredibly cool coffees.

Recent findings suggest that we are always on the hunt for roasters and subscriptions we haven’t tried. These are the ones that have landed in our grinders recently that we’re loving.

If you're into the idea of coffee drinking as a ritualistic ~experience~, Folk Coffee Club is for you. Founded by a Q-Grader, a.k.a. a sommelier for the coffee world, Folk specializes in rare coffees that score at least 86 points (in Q-Grader speak). Unlike many of the other coffee subscriptions on this list, Folk gives you zero options; instead, they'll send you one shipment every month with two expert-curated coffees.

In a recent development, tester: Alaina Chou What really sets Folk apart, though, are the intentional extras they included with each shipment. Along with the two coffees, each month features a piece of art, a curated playlist, some thought starters, and a tasting guide that elevate the mundane ritual of coffee brewing and drinking into a full-blown experience you're encouraged to slow down and savor. The whole package, coffees included, is meant to draw on a unifying theme.

Folk's first shipment, Volume 00, was titled “Off Script,” and featured two Gesha coffees—a distinctive varietal that takes supreme care to grow. Each coffee tasted unlike any other I've had, one with notes of jasmine and caramelized peach, the other reminiscent of blood orange and dark chocolate. The whole thing was beautifully packaged and felt like a luxurious gift to receive, the thoughtful intention behind each component highly evident.

The bottom line: Think of Folk like a monthly ritual, complete with art, a playlist, and rare coffees you won't find anywhere else. If you're the type to linger over your morning cup, this one's worth every penny.

In a recent development, there is no better proof point that the world of exquisitely roasted coffee beans has anchored itself absolutely everywhere than the Onyx Coffee Lab. Onyx was started by Jon and Andrea Allen (who would later become a U.S. barista champion) in Springdale, Arkansas, in the Ozarks, and as it has spread throughout the state, it has also become one of the most recognizable names in specialty coffee. Such is Onyx’s reputation that it’s bled over into other areas, landing the Rogers, Arkansas headquarters a nod as a James Beard Award finalist for the best bar program in America.

Tester: Noah Kaufman As for the coffee subscriptions themselves, they’re straightforward to set up: simply tick the box for quantity and the box for frequency. Onyx offers the reliable roaster’s choice option with a lot of interesting single origins and one-offs (I particularly liked a Rwandan washed coffee from Kanzu Station) that all include the most informative explainers I’ve ever seen attached to a bag of coffee. The cards include a breakdown of all the inputs that contribute to the cost, detailed brewing instructions for both pour-over and espresso, and an explanation of the fermentation and roasting process.

For people looking for more familiar flavors, Onyx has subscription options that combine a small amount of more adventurous beans like the Kanzu with its more familiar blends, letting curious drinkers dip their toes in something upcoming. And for a more special experience, Onyx releases a small number of memberships to what it calls “Echelon” for monthly deliveries of its rarest coffee.

Contemporary Coffee Subscription.

The Greenville, South Carolina roaster has grown now to have five cafes, a robust bakery and tea program, and some of the coolest, most beautiful branding in the coffee world. But it also has a wide range of blends and single-producer beans.

I first walked into Methodical’s café in Greenville in 2017 for a single origin pour-over, and at the time quick national shipping of fresh coffee was still in its early stages, so that stop didn’t end with me signing up for regular deliveries. But now the infrastructure is there and the coffee is great. Methodical sorts its coffee into three main buckets for three different types of coffee drinkers: classic (where you’ll find medium and dark roasts great for batch brewing and espresso), contemporary (where you’ll find medium roast coffees great for batch brewing or pour-over), and “avant-garde” (where you’ll find lighter roast coffees, sometimes fruity, sometimes tea-like, that are best enjoyed black).

Our editors have used every one of these coffee subscriptions in their homes over several months and some for years. We’ve made sure to try a variety of bean types where possible, and to try the beans with a variety of brewing methods to see how well they perform as espresso, pour-over, drip coffee, and French-pressed coffee.

Our editors are continually testing many of these services and constantly trying new coffee subscriptions to keep this list updated as the market changes, so be sure to check back as we update it often.

There are hundreds of coffee subscriptions out there, so we followed two guiding principles when selecting which subscriptions to test:.

Industry observers note that A coffee’s freshness has a huge impact on its flavor once brewed, no matter if you’re using a fancy espresso machine or a simple French press. The best subscription services will guarantee freshly roasted beans, either roasted to order or within a week or so of shipping.

According to recent reports, the other major factor in your coffee’s flavor is how recently the beans were ground. I’m a big advocate of ordering whole-bean coffee and grinding the beans just before brewing, so all of the options we tested offer that. (Of course, I know that many people may prefer the convenience of ground coffee. Most of the services below also offer that as an option, although my colleagues and I will continue to raise our eyebrows at you until you get a good coffee grinder.).

Tester: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor Best for: People who want high-quality coffee, but aren’t interested in choosing from a dizzying array of adventurous options.

Intelligentsia, out of Chicago, is one of the OG players in third-wave coffee (if you’re unfamiliar, "third wave" has a specific meaning, but is sometimes used as shorthand for a generation of coffee roasters deeply invested in quality, consistency, and unique flavors in coffee). Intelligentsia’s House Blend and Black Cat espresso roast have become staples at bakeries and coffee shops all over the country, and its subscription service gives you a regular supply of those two as well as its deeper catalog of different beans. There’s one single origin option, but the subscription itself is mostly based around Intelligentsia’s blends, which rotate seasonally.

This is a pretty simple, straightforward subscription. There is no quiz or process to determine what kind of coffee is “best for you”; rather, you just manually put in which subscription you want, choosing between the same blend (including espresso), rotating blends, or the roaster’s choice. You can also select how many times a month you want beans and how many bags you want per shipment. Changing to a different subscription is also quite easy. While you won’t find the same kind of personalized curation options as some of the other subscriptions on this list, Intelligentsia does offer one of the widest ranges of grind types if you aren’t getting whole bean coffee, running from the finest Turkish coffee grind to a super coarse (even coarser than cold brew) percolator grind.

Industry observers note that I got “Intelligentsia's Choice” because I’m a sucker for single-origin beans (and have had the opportunity to try all their classic blends already). The beans came from some of the strongholds of international coffee production: Ethiopia and Nicaragua. Making a carafe of pour-over coffee a day, enough for two people or one me, I used about one bag every two weeks. The most noteworthy coffee to me was a very fruity natural process Ethiopian coffee. After testing it extensively, I can tell you that this is a reliable, relatively affordable subscription; the Intelligentsia Classics subscription is only $17 a bag. It would be worthwhile for anyone who wants quality but isn’t trying to be too adventurous with their morning coffee.

Sources indicate that just to note, in 2015, Peet’s bought up a majority stake in Intelligentsia. I don’t think it has changed the quality of the coffee at all, but it is something worth being transparent about.

Tester: Carly Westerfield, associate manager of audience strategy Best for: Someone who likes high-quality beans and doesn’t know exactly what flavor they’re looking for, but might get overwhelmed by some of the multi-roaster options on this list.

It has been revealed that counter Culture is a longtime favorite roaster of many a BA staffer (food director Chris Morocco included). It has storefronts in several major cities, and you can find Counter Culture’s coffee in stores across the country, but they also offer several subscription options online.

According to recent reports, I had a really easy time ordering the coffee. There aren’t endless options to choose from, which is nice because subscriptions like these can sometimes be a lot to manage. Because I wanted to see a variety of beans, there were only two: the Single-Origin Subscription and the Blend Box. I opted for the latter. As someone who’s often overwhelmed by choices, I always appreciate a curated shopping experience where there are fewer things to choose from and therefore fewer things to compare, contrast, and potentially have buyer’s remorse over. I did struggle a little to figure out how to end the subscription; Counter Culture makes that part a little trickier than everything else.

In a recent development, this subscription sends two different blends (12-oz. bags) at a time at a frequency of your choosing. Options there ranged from every week to every eight weeks, and the ability to change this post-purchase was clear. The Blend Box subscription pulls from six blend options ranging from light to dark roast, plus any “seasonal blend’ they have available, so you will end up seeing the same beans after about four deliveries. Shipping was fast and the email communication from CC made it so I always knew when I was being charged and when the box would be shipped and delivered.

While trying out this subscription, I received four different coffee blends: Iridescent Winter Blend, Significant Trouble, Fast Forward, and Forty-Six. At home, I use a Moccamaster Thermal Carafe Coffee Brewer and a Baratza Encore Coffee Grinder. With each of the blends I received, I was able to use the same measurements that I always use (9 g of coffee per 6 oz. of water) and found the coffee to be the right strength for me. Each blend has spot-on tasting notes provided as well. Overall, while the flavor profiles were totally different, none were overwhelmingly bitter or acidic—a big no-no in my book. These coffees all had a really well-rounded, almost creamy quality to them that actually resulted in me using way less half-and-half than I normally take in my coffee. By far my favorite blend is, sadly, the limited edition Iridescent Winter Blend. Big Trouble came in a close second.

This subscription is great for someone who likes high-quality beans but doesn’t know exactly what flavor they’re looking for—perhaps, for instance, a recent college grad who’s been drinking coffee for years but hasn’t had to buy it for their own home yet. The ability to pause or change how often the deliveries come also makes it nice for someone who might travel often or need to have more coffee on hand at random times (maybe they have frequent house guests?).

Tester: Maria Paz Mendez Hodes, director of creative development Best for: Eager-to-learn beginners.

In a recent development, stumptown is a Portland, OR–based roaster that’s been around since 1999. It offers three subscription options: Roaster’s Choice, Blend Shuffle, and Favorite on Repeat. As a novice coffee brewer, I wished there were a little more elaboration on the differences between Roaster’s Choice and Blend Shuffle. In the end I opted for the Roaster’s Choice, which promised to be a tour of seasonal, single-origin, and occasionally rare coffees, changing every two weeks.

Recent findings suggest that I wasn’t 100% sure until the bag revealed up at my door that I was ordering whole beans versus ground coffee. To some that may be glaringly obvious, but just another reminder that the site did not seem aimed at rank beginners like me. From what I can tell, Stumptown subscriptions are all whole-bean-only. Beyond that, the ordering process was clear and easy! My first bag arrived three days after ordering, and the next one almost exactly on schedule.

A guilty confession: We keep breaking the Hario V60 carafe that I use to make pour-over, and I’ve gotten hooked on the extravagant convenience of bottled cold brew. The arrival of the Stumptown beans was exciting enough that we couldn’t wait for a replacement to arrive from Amazon, so we improvised by setting the dripper over a mason jar. Unglamorous setup aside, the first brew was an immediate reminder of the sense pleasures of the morning coffee ritual, dramatically amplified by using the fanciest beans I’d ever purchased. The freshness of the seasonal beans was obvious upon opening the package—they were lustrous and almost oily, with juicy notes that I’ve rarely detected in the supermarket brands near me. I don’t have a highly attuned coffee nose, but I could certainly taste distinct differences between the bags I received: light, bright fruit in the Montes de Oro from Costa Rica and deep caramel and spice in the Duramina from Ethiopia.

There were blurbs on the back of each bag sketching details about the coffee producers (e.g., how long they’d partnered with Stumptown and some unique features of their agricultural operations). It’s a good initiation for an interested newbie, but I think a coffee enthusiast could still glean quite a bit from these brief details. The one addition I would have loved would have been a card in the box with some deeper insights connecting the tasting notes and flavors to the processes and places mentioned. While there were tasting notes on the website for “Pick of the Week,” the coffee described wasn’t one I had received—another argument for a card in the box.

Tester: Travis Rainey, staff photographer/visuals editor Best for: People who like a little personality in their morning coffee.

I was tempted to choose a curveball and select the espresso subscription, but opted for a more American coffee experience this time. I chose to test the Curated Single Origin subscription, which sends you a different single-origin coffee bean each week. The first bag of beans I received was from Concepción Huista, just north of Huehuetenango in western Guatemala. It was a very light, almost delicate kind of coffee. I had to adjust the grinder setting to a finer coffee ground to make the coffee a little more bold. For the most part, I make coffee with a pour-over method. A new coffee arrives each week, so the next selection was from Abana Estate near Jimma in southwestern Ethiopia. This has been my favorite coffee to make so far. It's distinctive, spiced, but still goes down smooth. The third variety is Panangan Mata from Aceh on the northern tip of Sumatra in Indonesia. I’ve only had one cup yet, but it’s fruity, which is a fun surprise.

In general, I’ve found that each Equator coffee has had a distinct personality, making this subscription ideal for people who want to have opinions about coffee—the beans here are the kind that sort of demand one of you. I also appreciate that the containers the coffee beans come in feature detailed, but succinct information on where the coffee is coming from.

Tester: Hana Asbrink, deputy food director Best for: Both novice and experienced coffee drinkers alike who want their coffee selections handled for them.

My ordering experience was straightforward. I chose the Roaster’s Choice Subscription, so I didn’t know what I’d be getting first. My first bag (Honduras San Francisco whole beans) had a roast date just three days before it arrived at my house, so you can’t get much fresher than that. I appreciated this first blind bean as I’m not sure I would have chosen it for myself based on my personal preferences. I used a medium grind on the whole beans for my drip coffee maker. I’m curious to see how I’ll enjoy it pulled in the big boy coffee maker as an Americano.

Recent findings suggest that the bag touts tasting notes of strawberry, raspberry, and dark chocolate, which are spot-on. The first whiff gave me a fruit-and-nut chocolate bar, and the taste matches in a delicate way with a touch some floral undertones.

Tester: Carina Finn Best for: Best for someone with a high-end caffeine routine.

It has been revealed that you can find a Blue Bottle café in most major cities—the brand makes a reliably great cup of coffee, whether you’re into fruity pour-overs or sophisticated seasonal lattes. Blue Bottle’s coffee subscription makes it easy to recreate that experience at home. It has around 10 different subscription options for things like instant espresso and matcha powders to rotating single-origin offerings and subscriptions tailored to specific roast level preferences.

Tester: Alaina Chou Best for: Someone looking for seasonality in their coffee.

It has been revealed that sightglass is a coffee-shop-slash-roaster based in San Francisco. They offer subscriptions for all of the coffees in their regular lineup if you find a fave you want to stick to, but we’d recommend trying out one of their rotating options to get a taste for all the brand has to offer. That leaves you with either the Blend Shuffle or the Seasonal Variety subscription. The ordering process is simple: Just select which subscription you want, how much coffee you want in each shipment (12 ounces, 2 pounds, or 5 pounds), what kind of grind you want, and how often you’d like to receive deliveries.

Recent findings suggest that one of the things I like about Sightglass, as opposed to some other coffee shop-roaster hybrids, is that they regularly introduce new single-origin coffees, which might feature in that seasonal subscription. You can also opt in to get notified about any new drops through the Sightglass Batches text-to-order service.

According to recent reports, I'm partial to Sightglass’s Blueboon blend. It's a medium roast with notes of milk chocolate, mandarin, and honeysuckle that I quite enjoy brewed as espresso and used in my morning iced latte. It’s beautifully balanced, and the components get changed seasonally to retain the right ratio of sweetness, body, and acidity.

Tester: Alaina Chou Best for: People who want to hone their coffee-tasting skills.

In a recent development, if you dream of being able to approach the coffee world with sommelier-like expertise but you aren’t quite there yet, a Driftaway coffee subscription will help. Driftaway is an immigrant-owned, woman-led roastery based in Brooklyn, NY, and it’s the only service we’ve tried that starts out with a blind tasting. When you go to place your first order, you’ll have the option to choose between light roast, medium, and dark roasts, or espresso (which each include two or three different 4-oz. bags of coffee to blind taste test), or opt for the Explorer Box, which includes five different coffees spanning all roast levels.

If the tasting aspect of this service appeals to you, I’d recommend going with the Explorer Box option. Each initial Explorer Box comes with five mystery coffees, a wheel with flavor notes, a tasting form, and an envelope revealing the identities of your coffees. Driftaway offers weekly virtual tasting classes free of charge, but if you’d rather taste on your own time, they also have prerecorded tasting tutorials available on their website. Regardless of whether you opt for the Explorer Box or a roast-specific subscription, after your initial order, you’ll give feedback on which coffee you preferred in order to inform your future shipments. Many coffee companies even give you the option to send the farmer feedback, which I appreciated.

Along with the Explorer Box, I also tried out the espresso subscription. I was partial to the Burundi Turihamwe and Guatemala Ella blend, which was wonderfully nutty and had notes of milk chocolate and stone fruits. I loved being able to read more about the women farmers behind this blend and trace the story of the coffee from harvest to brewing, a feature that’s in keeping with Driftaway’s overall ethos.

Founded in 2015 in NYC's East Village, Coffee Project NY has grown from a single café into a full operation spanning retail, roasting, wholesale, and education. Owner Chi Sum Ngai is a certified Q grader and roasting championship competitor who personally oversees the roasting program, sourcing from small-scale cooperatives and family farms committed to improving conditions for workers.

In a recent development, tester: Olivia Tarantino, senior commerce editor The subscription is straightforward: select the Roaster's Choice Single Origin Subscription and receive one to three 10-oz. bags one to two times a month. Coffee Project New York is not shy about its credentials; each bag arrives with tasting notes, farm sourcing, processing methods, and MASL (metres above sea level, which indicates the altitude at which beans were grown and profoundly impacts flavor). My standout was the Cabra Noir Wush Wush from the Competition Series, a runner-up at Mexico's prestigious AMCCE competition. Produced through anaerobic fermentation, I hand-ground the beans for a Hario pour-over and was met with such vivid guava notes that I double-checked the bag to make sure it wasn't a cofermentation. It wasn't. It was just that good.

Bottom line: Any coffee drinker will appreciate the expertly sourced beans, but this is a subscription where nerds can truly geek out, sampling rare cultivars and competition-level coffees from around the world.

Wonderstate Coffee (Single Origin).

Wonderstate Coffee Blend Shuffle).

Wonderstate Coffee (Roaster's Choice).

A certified B-Corporation with a fully solar-powered roastery, a transparent farmer payment model, and a novel profit-sharing model, Viroqua-based Wonderstate has gained a lot of goodwill for its business practices, but it also makes really good coffee.

Tester: Noah Kaufman Admittedly, this is a bit of a homer pick, as I have long thought Wonderstate to be the preeminent coffee roaster from my beloved home state of Wisconsin. But for those of you not lucky enough to be from Wisconsin, you should get to know them too. Twice named roaster of the year by Roast magazine (which is probably how it ended up as part of the Podium Coffee subscription), Wonderstate regularly has delicious, clean limited edition single origins—I like to get them as part of the single origin flight subscription. The subscriptions themselves come in a few varieties. The single-origin flight delivers three 100-gram packages of Wonderstate’s rarer coffees every two weeks. Roaster’s choice delivers a different single-origin coffee at an interval of your choosing. And the single coffee subscription gives you a regular delivery of the Wonderstate blend of your choosing, if you’re the type who wants more consistency of flavor in your morning cup.

Industry observers note that the bottom line: Wonderstate makes excellent coffee and runs an ethical business, which is a combination that's rarer than it should be. If you care about where your money goes as much as what's in your cup, this is the subscription for you.

Black & White Roasters (1-Bag Specialty Subscription).

Black & White Roasters (1-Bag Year Round Subscription).

If you find most black coffee off-putting, you might still love an unadulterated cup from Raleigh, North Carolina’s Black and White Coffee Roasters. Started by two American barista champions, Black and White are masters of the funky and fruity, with lots of experiments in co-fermented coffee (a process that uses actual fruit) and anaerobic fermented coffee (which produces very pronounced fruit notes).

Sources indicate that tester: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor It can be a very hands-off subscription. The only required information is whether you want one or two bags at a time and the frequency you need your coffee (anywhere between one and six weeks). Black and White will take care of the rest. If you do see a bag on their website you like, you can add it to your queue; otherwise, the team in North Carolina will select for you.

Every bag I received was of a funky variety, using ingredients like passion fruit, but they produce a number of more classic flavor profiles, which are available as part of their “year-round” subscription; the year-round is also about 20% cheaper than a subscription with the specialty bags.

The bottom line: If you're drawn to funky, fruit-forward coffee but don't want to think too hard about what to order next, Black and White is the subscription for you. Just set your frequency and let the barista champions decide.

Bean Box is focused on the “curation” experience. The service’s tasting team offers what they claim is the largest selection of specialty coffee online, with over 600 different brews in its rolodex. The selection is sourced from dozens of small-batch, sustainably focused roasters from around the country—meaning you could likely go years without tasting coffee from the same roaster twice.

Tester: Dan Siegel, head of video Starting my subscription was exceptionally easy and clear. I appreciated the option to tailor the subscription to my own tastes: Bean Box asked me to choose among Light & Bright, Medium & Cozy, Dark & Toasty, Espresso, or Decaf. For this run, I selected the Curators' Choice option, marketed as the curation team’s seasonal favorites and a mix of newly introduced and old coffees. There is an app available to manage subscriptions and read lengthy details on each roaster or track the origin of your beans.

In a recent development, this subscription was not designed to save me money on coffee; this is for enthusiasts. My first bag from “Gimme! Coffee,” out of Ithaca, NY, hit hard on the Bean Box mission: The roaster is employee-owned, shipping fair trade beans from Coopfam, Brazil’s first certified fair trade coffee grower. This was a standout for any time of day as a medium-bodied brew, subtly sweet with virtually no bitterness or acidity via my automatic OXO 8-cup machine or my Hario V60 pour-over. My second bag, La Cumbre from Little City in Austin, was a bit too bright and fruity for my taste, advertising caramel, mango, and green apple tasting notes—but this was the path I chose with the Curator’s Choice option.

The bottom line: If you have the means, get the beans. I would keep this going for years if money were no object. The money seems to be going toward roasters that align with my values. One of my values is delicious coffee. But also treating workers at every stop along the way like human beings.

In a recent development, if receiving personalized coffee picks from a catalogue of nearly 600 coffees from 60 different roasters sounds like your cup of tea (or, rather, joe), then I will point you toward MistoBox. I found a lot to love about this service after testing it for several months, particularly the way Misto tailored its selections to me and my taste.

Tester: Alaina Chou, commerce writer The ordering process starts with a quiz covering your preferences: how you take your coffee, roast level, whole or ground beans, and frequency. But what sets MistoBox apart is what comes after: a second, more detailed quiz where you share how you brew, how you grind, and any other specifics to help the team dial in your order. The whole process feels genuinely personal, and that expert-curated aspect is, to me, the other major perk that makes a subscription worth it in the first place.

It has been revealed that I’ve loved every coffee MistoBox has sent me so far. The first shipment was the Roma Espresso Blend from Parisi Artisan Coffee, which was aptly described as having notes of milk chocolate, almond, and honeysuckle. I tend to drink espresso, most often with milk in a cappuccino made using my Breville Oracle Jet. The Roma blend, which MistoBox sent me based on that information, worked beautifully for this.

It has been revealed that after you receive each coffee, you’ll have the chance to rate it out of five and leave any tasting notes, which you can share with your curators if you’d like. Coffees you’ve tried show up in a customer dashboard, as will your “Brew Queue,” a.k.a. the lineup of the next coffees coming to your door. These will appear as “MistoBox’s choice” by default, but if you loved a coffee you tried and want it again, or spy a coffee in their collection that you’d like to request, you can opt to add specific coffees to your queue as well. Anyone looking for some expert guidance in discovering latest coffees from roasters all over the country will enjoy MistoBox.

The bottom line: MistoBox’s user-friendly interface and extensive feedback options make it a great choice for anyone looking for some expert guidance in discovering new coffees from roasters all over the country.

Are coffee subscriptions worth it?

If you’re a frequent coffee drinker, the answer is probably yes. Whether you have a favorite blend you find yourself buying on repeat or you’re eager to try newly introduced beans and hone your tasting skills, a coffee subscription will make your life easier and may even save you some money. If you’re presently buying a bag of beans every few weeks at your local coffee shop or grocery store, that bag could potentially be cheaper when bought on subscription—and you’ll get the added convenience of never needing to worry about restocking your stash.

How do coffee subscriptions work?

At the most basic level, a coffee subscription works much like any other subscription service: You select a quantity and frequency, and lo and behold, a bag of freshly roasted coffee shows up at your doorstep every one to four weeks, depending what you chose. But no one wants to come home from vacation to a pile of beans that are past their prime, only to receive another package the following day. So these coffee subscriptions make it easy to put your coffee deliveries on hold, or cancel them altogether. Some also offer personalization in the form of quizzes or feedback forms, so you can know you're getting a curated selection that’s tailored specifically to your tastes.

How much coffee should you order?

Many of the subscriptions on this list will let you customize your delivery frequency and bag quantity to best accommodate your household size and coffee drinking habits. Ideally, you’ll want to hit a sweet spot where you're using up nearly all of your beans by the time the next shipment comes. To figure out the right amount of coffee for you, you’ll need to do a little math:.

If instant coffee is more your speed, we don’t blame you—it’s hard to beat the convenience. And while instant coffee has historically gotten a bad wrap from third-wave coffee nerds and espresso heads everywhere, you’d be surprised what innovations have been made in the space in recent years. After tasting a whopping 40, we found a range of great-tasting options that would impress even the most seasoned coffee pro. Head this way for our review of all the best instant coffees and espressos money can buy.

Now that you’ve read all about the best coffee subscription services out there, it’s time to upgrade that old drip coffee machine or invest in a upcoming espresso setup.

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, here at a hearing in July, has won a sixth term representing the 9th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Recent findings suggest that florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

Industry observers note that soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

In a recent development, house Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s newly introduced Republican-drawn map.

Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The fresh map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

According to recent reports, “Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida showed voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto said in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”.

While Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Julia Child's solution to a common turkey dilemma was equal parts culinary brilliance and holiday theater.
  • It has been revealed that julia Child had a marvelous way of making even the most intimidating cooking techniques seem entirely within reach.
  • According to recent reports, take Thanksgiving turkey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Julia Child's solution to a common turkey dilemma was equal parts culinary brilliance and holiday theater.

It has been revealed that julia Child had a marvelous way of making even the most intimidating cooking techniques seem entirely within reach. She was a brilliant cook, a gifted teacher, and a woman who understood that a little butter could solve an astonishing number of problems. But perhaps her greatest talent was her willingness to question the rules, even when those rules involved one of America’s most beloved holiday traditions.

According to recent reports, take Thanksgiving turkey. Most of us have spent our lives roasting the bird whole, partly because that’s how it’s always been done and partly because a beautifully browned turkey makes such a magnificent centerpiece on a holiday table. Julia, however, recognized a rather inconvenient flaw in this arrangement: A whole turkey is not well designed for even cooking.

Sources indicate that her solution was ingenious. She took the turkey apart, cooked its individual pieces, and then put the whole thing back together again for presentation. It was a triumph of culinary common sense, with just enough theatrical flair to make the whole thing unmistakably Julia.

Julia called her creation the “re-assembled roast turkey,” a technique she shared in her cookbook, The Way to Cook. Rather than wrestling an entire bird into the oven and hoping for the best, she removed the backbone, separated the leg and thigh portions, and roasted the breast on a bed of stuffing while the dark meat cooked in another pan.

Once everything was properly cooked, she arranged the pieces together on a serving platter, restoring the turkey to something resembling its original form. In her recipe, Julia cheerfully suggested that nobody would ever know the difference.

Recent findings suggest that in a 2012 NPR Thanksgiving segment, Christopher Kimball, who had cooked alongside Julia, demonstrated the method with host Renee Montagne. The two had a wonderful time discussing the reconstructed bird, which they affectionately dubbed “Frankenturkey.” It wasn’t quite traditional, but that was rather the point. Julia had found a way to preserve the spectacle of a whole roasted turkey without actually having to cook one.

It has been revealed that the trouble with roasting a whole turkey is that its various parts have very different needs. The breast is lean and can become dry and stringy when overcooked, while the legs and thighs contain more fat and connective tissue, and generally benefit from cooking to a higher internal temperature. Getting everything just right at the same time is a challenge, even for experienced cooks.

Breaking down the turkey solves much of that problem. With the pieces separated, you can monitor their temperatures individually and remove them as they finish cooking. The dark meat has time to become tender without drying out the breast, and heat circulates more efficiently around the smaller pieces, reducing the overall roasting time.

It’s a method we’ve championed at Taste of Home. Our guide to cooking a deconstructed turkey outlines the process of breaking down the bird, roasting the individual pieces and getting beautifully crisp skin. You can even ask your butcher to handle the disassembly if you’d rather not begin Thanksgiving morning with a pair of poultry shears.

And there’s another advantage Julia certainly appreciated: With the backbone removed, you’ve already got a head start on making a rich turkey stock for the gravy.

Of course, there’s no requirement that you follow Julia all the way through to the reconstruction. You can simply arrange the carved meat on a serving platter and bring it to the table. But I do love that Julia went to the trouble of putting her turkey back together. She understood that Thanksgiving dinner is as much about tradition and presentation as it is about good cooking, and she found a wonderfully clever way to have both.

Industry observers note that the result was better-tasting turkey that still got its moment of glory on the table. And if anyone could make taking a turkey apart and putting it back together seem like the most sensible thing in the world, it was Julia Child.

The Secret to the Creamiest Mac and Cheese Comes in a Can

  • Sources indicate that I’ve made enough macaroni and cheese over the years to have developed some fairly strong opinions about it.
  • Industry observers note that which is why I’m particularly fond of a method that requires just three ingredients: pasta, grated cheese and evaporated milk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Making a truly excellent bowl of mac and cheese shouldn't take an entire afternoon. Here's the one ingredient I rely on to get the creamiest cheese sauce every time.

Sources indicate that I’ve made enough macaroni and cheese over the years to have developed some fairly strong opinions about it. Having two kids has given me plenty of opportunities to experiment, from throwing together the familiar blue box to baking versions that require several kinds of cheese and a considerable amount of attention. I appreciate a proper cheese sauce as much as anyone, but there are evenings when dirtying another saucepan to make a roux and standing over the stove with a whisk feels like an unreasonable amount of ceremony for a bowl of macaroni.

Industry observers note that which is why I’m particularly fond of a method that requires just three ingredients: pasta, grated cheese and evaporated milk. It produces an exceptionally creamy mac and cheese without butter, flour or any of the usual fuss, and it’s so simple that even boxed mac begins to look complicated.

It has been revealed that evaporated milk is regular milk that’s been heated until about 60% of its water is gone. The result is thicker and more concentrated than ordinary milk, with a richness that makes it especially useful for cheese sauces.

More importantly, those concentrated milk proteins help the cheese melt into a smooth, cohesive sauce. Ordinarily, adding cheese directly to hot liquid can be a temperamental business. The fat may separate, the proteins can tighten up, and the sauce can become grainy instead of silky. Evaporated milk helps keep everything together, doing much of the work that a traditional flour-and-butter roux would otherwise accomplish.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

One of the things I like most about this method is how little precision it demands. If you’re cooking a pound of macaroni, start with a 12-ounce can of evaporated milk and roughly 12 to 16 ounces of grated cheese. Sharp cheddar provides plenty of flavor, while Monterey Jack or fontina will give you a smooth melt. I generally prefer a combination, but there’s no reason to make a special trip to the store if you already have a perfectly good block of cheese in the refrigerator.

I do recommend grating the cheese yourself, since the anti-caking ingredients in bagged shredded cheese can keep it from melting smoothly. Beyond that, there’s plenty of room for flexibility. There’s no need to measure everything down to the last ounce, which is part of what makes this method so wonderful.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

According to recent reports, boil the pasta in generously salted water as you normally would, then strain it and return it to the pot, reserving about a cup of pasta water. Add the cheese and evaporated milk, warming them gently over low heat. Keep stirring until everything melts into a smooth sauce, adding splashes of pasta water as you go until it reaches your desired consistency.

Industry observers note that the same trick works beautifully in more elaborate recipes, whether you’re making a baked southern mac and cheese, a massive pan of potluck mac and cheese or a comforting crockpot mac and cheese. All have their merits, but for an ordinary weeknight, I rather like knowing that one pot, three ingredients, and about as much time as it takes to boil pasta are all I need.

“Chaats are a mighty snack that tell India’s culinary story more adeptly than any other food,” writes Nashville-based Indian chef Maneet Chauhan in her cookbook Chaat. She reminisces about a fruity street snack sold by a chaat vendor near the Hyderabadi train station. Sweet pineapple, tangy lime juice, sour-salty chaat masala, chile powder, cilantro, and pomegranate seeds created what she describes as “a decadent mosaic of colors and plucky flavors.” Chauhan suggests swapping in ripe mango or watermelon when in season, or drizzling the finished dish with lightly salted yogurt for added richness and depth. Serve as a snack, or as a side dish for barbecued meats or seafood.

  • Sources indicate that to go one step further, home safes rated as fireproof will protect your belongings from house fires and sprinkler systems, but if you're looking for protection from natural disasters, there are solutions out there.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, A good home safe will protect your most important items from theft and damage, but if you want one that will also offer protection from heat, direct flames, and even water (in some cases), you need a fireproof home safe. This protection isn’t just limited to non-flammable items like jewelry or firearms, either. High-quality fireproof safes keep cash, important documents, photographs, and passports safe, too.

Sources indicate that to go one step further, home safes rated as fireproof will protect your belongings from house fires and sprinkler systems, but if you're looking for protection from natural disasters, there are solutions out there. A safe rated for extreme temperatures will safeguard your things in the event of a wildfire, and those with airtight seals should prevent water from seeping in even during a flash flood.

We’ve reviewed the best fireproof home safes below with picks that cover your needs regardless of what you’re storing or how much space you need.

We made our choices on this list based on extensive research, looking closely at key features, brand reputation, and of course, each model’s temperature and fireproof rating. We also looked through customer reviews, making note of how well their safes held up in real-world situations. Beyond this, we took into account recommendations from professional firefighters. Because of these factors, you won’t see a wide variety of brands on this list.

Industry observers note that in previous versions of this article, we featured fire safes and chests that were tested out by our team. While these models have since been discontinued or are out of stock, we used this experience to inform new choices for this list. All the safes on this list are “true” fireproof options, meaning that the safe itself will hold up, not just an included fireproof envelope. Each safe we selected is rated to withstand temperatures of at least 1,200 degrees Fahrenheit.

More to Explore: Best Outdoor Security Cameras • Best Video Doorbell Cameras • Best Carbon Monoxide Detectors • Best Smart Locks.

As you’ll see throughout this list, we believe in SentrySafe as a top brand for fireproof safes—for its lifetime warranty, $50,000 fire protection guarantee, and reliably high levels of fire protection across all products. This mid-sized, 1.23-cubic-foot option is the perfect choice for most people.

Alongside a fire rating of up to 1,700 degrees F for a full hour, the safe boasts a fully waterproof design that protects internal items completely for up to 24 hours in up to 8 inches of submerged water.

It has been revealed that beyond the powerful protection it offers, the fireproof safe also has internal organization features like key hooks, a shelf, and a lockable drawer for especially valuable items. The interior of the safe is even lit to help you see inside. That said, both the lights and the digital keypad are battery-operated, so you'll need to periodically replace them.

The safe, as a whole, weighs close to 90 pounds. While this is a great deterrent from a thief trying to simply steal the entire safe, it can make it quite difficult install or carry up stairs on your own.

As an affordable yet durable alternative to some of the higher-end models on our list, this safe from Amazon Basics checks a lot of our boxes. At 1.24 cubic feet, it's actually slightly larger than our Best Overall choice from SentrySafe, leaving you with just as much space inside, including a top shelf for organization.

The safe also comes with a digital keyboard for easy access. If the keyboard is damaged during a fire, the safe also comes with a backup emergency key that unlocks the mechanism manually.

It has been revealed that the biggest detractor for this safe is its durability. The safe is only rated to handle up to 1,200 F for 20 minutes. This is considerably lower than many other safes on this list both in temperature and duration.

Recent findings suggest that if you require more space and organization than our previous recommendations, this safe provides plenty. With over 2 cubic feet of space, there is significantly more room to store larger valuables, such as photo albums or antiques.

Furthermore, the internal organization boasts a top tray and a large bottom drawer, as well as key hooks and a small storage cubby on the door. Unlike other models on this list, the safe uses a dial lock which doesn't require batteries, but it can be cumbersome to use.

Like all SentrySafe models, this one will protect your items for up to an hour at 1,700 F and prevent moisture damage for 24 hours in 8 inches of water. This impressive durability extends to the outer strength of the safe, as well, which can handle a fall from 15 feet without significant damage. Because of its size and strength, the safe weighs a hefty 125 pounds.

Unlike the more traditional safes we recommend, this option from SentrySafe functions more like a secure file cabinet than a traditional safe. The chest holds up to 40 hanging files for easy document organization and has a small space on the lid for handheld items like passports or electronics.

Sources indicate that while the safe gives up some fire protection compared to the classic options on our list (it’s rated for 30 minutes at 1,550 degrees), it more than makes up for this with its robust water protection. The file storage box can be fully submerged in water for up to 72 hours without the items inside seeing any water damage at all.

At 39 pounds, this safe is slightly more portable than the bulkier home options, though it is still relatively cumbersome to transport given the lack of handles or wheels.

This Sanctuary model stands out as the gold standard for fire protection. It’s capable of withstanding a blistering 1,800 F for 90 minutes. That makes it the best home safe to protect your valuables from the extreme heat of wildfires.

Sources indicate that additionally, with ETL-rated waterproofing, it can hold out for 7 days in up to 6 inches of standing water. The company also provides a lifetime warranty against fire, natural flood, and theft.

The LED-lit interior has two upholstered shelves and is California DOJ-certified for firearm storage. For security, the electronic lock has a timed lockout mode and tamper indicator. You can also enable an optional silent entry mode for added discretion.

In a recent development, once you get this compact safe situated, at over 62 pounds, it’s not likely you’ll want to move it again. But, its sturdiness and heavy-duty construction are worth the extra money.

It has been revealed that if you only need to protect a few small items, like your passport, a USB drive, and some jewelry, there’s no need to invest in such a large safe. This lock box safe from SentrySafe is small enough to be hidden away on a shelf in your closet, but it doesn’t sacrifice fire protection in the name of being compact.

It has been revealed that rated to handle up to 1,550 degrees F for up to 30 minutes, the lock box should be able to withstand house fires without much matter. The carrying handle also makes it easy to take this safe with you if you are evacuating the fire quickly.

Recent findings suggest that of course, because of its small size, there’s no internal organization. Everything just sits in the same compartment. But it’s not a feature-less safe. If you are interested in additional theft prevention, it comes with a bolt-down kit for securing the safe to your floor.

Sources indicate that for security beyond just the physical integrity of the safe, the Mycube offers a biometric fingerprint scanner as the primary way to unlock its door. The safe saves up to 10 unique fingerprint IDs, so you can program it to open for you and your immediate family with ease.

If someone else needs access to the safe, you can also program a backup password they’ll enter from the digital keypad. Internally, the safe has a removable drawer for storing documents, small valuables, and watches. This also leaves the main compartment of the safe open for larger items.

Sources indicate that the Mycube fire safe is quite durable with the company claiming it is capable of withstanding 1,700 F for up to an hour. Its worth noting that Mysafe does not use UL for its fire rating, though the company does report that the rating it has would be the equivalent of one from UL.

Sources indicate that to withstand high temperatures, choose a safe that is completely fireproof rather than a security safe with a fire-resistant envelope. Unless all of your valuables fit comfortably in a fire-resistant envelope, the risk of damage to other items in the safe is far too high. Even in the envelope, your items will not be protected to the same degree as a completely fireproof safe.

Recent findings suggest that for advanced protection, fireproof safes should withstand temperatures of at least 1,150 F for 30 minutes or more. In the case of wildfire risk, a fireproof safe that protects at temperatures up to 1,800 F is your best protection. Keep in mind, though, that wildfires get as hot as 2,000 degrees, which would melt most of the safes included here. Any safe you purchase should have fireproof ratings certified by either the Underwriter’s Laboratory (UL) or the inspection firm Intertek, designated by an “ETL” mark.

In a recent development, there are several different types of locking mechanisms available depending on the level of security you desire. Among our recommendations, you’ll find models with traditional keys, combination locks, and electronic keypads. Some safes also come with biometric locks that only unlock to your specific fingerprint, which may offer an additional layer of security.

The size of the valuables you need to store and the available space in your home will dictate the ideal dimensions for your fireproof safe. Look for a deeper safe if you need to protect a large cache of valuables or a variety of different-sized items.

Industry observers note that some smaller safes, like the Honeywell Small Safe Box Chest, are shaped like briefcases and work best for holding key documents. Similarly, if you are looking to store jewelry, look for deeper safes equipped with drawers or trays to better organize your items.

Recent findings suggest that for a fireproof safe you can transport, look for a fireproof chest or document box that weighs 30 pounds or less. These safes are also light enough to be placed on a shelf. Heavier fireproof home security safes (upwards of 75 pounds and designed to deter thieves) usually specify and provide hardware for floor mounting.

Industry observers note that many fireproof safes that are water-resistant or waterproof may only be so under certain conditions, such as standing water of 5 to 8 inches, and possibly for only a certain duration of time. This ensures added protection of the safe’s contents when sprinklers go off in an apartment complex, or if the safe is in the direct line of heavy-duty hoses. Some fireproof security boxes or chests offer waterproof ratings anywhere from 8 to 72 hours spent submerged, which are optimal for homeowners who may face flood risks.

Sources indicate that fireproof rating is easily the most important feature to consider. An independent testing agency must rate the safe, and it should be able to withstand temperatures of at least 1,200 F. However, we recommend much higher for those who are worried about wildfires.

It has been revealed that beware of home security safes that companies list as fireproof, but aren't rated by a testing agency. Many of these safes do not have fireproof bodies and instead just include a small fire-resistant envelope to store sensitive items in.

Once the temperature on the safe interior gets above 350 F, any paper inside (including all your hard-earned cash) is at risk of scorching. Even rooms in a burning house that aren’t on fire can get above 600 degrees F at eye level, which is definitely hot enough to soften steel.

In a recent development, there are many things you can and should keep in a fireproof safe, but if it you need to keep the items chilled or temperature controlled, it shouldn’t go in the safe long term. Avoid storing volatile chemicals or batteries in a safe as they can deteriorate or spill and damage other valuables.

It has been revealed that you might assume most safes are lock it and forget it, but they do require some maintenance. You should “air out” your safe to avoid moisture build-up every few weeks to a few months depending on the climate where you live and the contents of your safe. You should also replace the batteries in battery-powered safe locks once a year.

Avoid installing a safe in the master bedroom, where security experts indicate thieves are most likely to check for valuables first. Fireproof safes are heavy, so it’s preferable to store them on the floor even though it might make it harder for you to access.

In fact, large standing safes often have mounting hardware included so you can bolt them into the floor of your basement or garage for additional security and stability.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

According to recent reports, “Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s key that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”.

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Recent findings suggest that before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

Recent findings suggest that “This has never been anything against John Thune,” said Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”.

According to recent reports, “Part of the glitch here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Industry observers note that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., stated voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

In a recent development, “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul noted.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

Sources indicate that “Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they remarked, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

According to recent reports, sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Moreno mentioned, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”.

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., mentioned on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”.

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides remarked.

It has been revealed that “It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

It has been revealed that that long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune remarked he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”.

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

It has been revealed that “If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

The secret to a beautifully golden Thanksgiving pie might be the simplest ingredient in your kitchen.

Thanksgiving pies have a way of bringing out the perfectionist in even the most relaxed bakers. Yet you might spend half an hour creating the perfect pie dough design, carefully crimping the edges or cutting little leaves from scraps of pastry, only to pull the finished pie from the oven and discover that your beautiful handiwork has browned unevenly. It’s a small disappointment in the grand scheme of things, but after all that effort, a little indignation is understandable.

An egg wash is supposed to give pastry a lovely golden color and delicate sheen, but getting it to cooperate isn’t always as simple as beating an egg and picking up a pastry brush. Fortunately, there’s an easy trick that makes a noticeable difference, and it comes courtesy of a familiar face in the baking world: Great British Baking Show judge Paul Hollywood.

Paul’s secret is simply to add a pinch of salt to the beaten egg. He lets it sit for about five minutes before brushing it onto pastry dough. In a BBC Food demonstration, Paul uses the technique to glaze scones, but it works just as well for giving pie crusts a beautiful, even finish.

Sources indicate that beat an egg with a small pinch of salt until they’re well combined, then set the mixture aside for a few minutes. Give it another quick stir before brushing a thin, even layer over the pastry. The amount of salt won’t affect the flavor, and there’s no reason to make any other adjustments to your favorite pie recipe.

Sources indicate that the difference is subtle but useful. Instead of clinging stubbornly to your pastry brush or collecting in the little crevices of a crimped edge, the egg wash spreads more easily.

Emiko Franzen For Taste Of Home.

If you’ve ever tried brushing a plain beaten egg onto pastry, you’ve probably noticed that it can be surprisingly thick and stringy. That’s because the proteins in the egg give it structure—a nuisance if you need to spread it evenly. Adding salt loosens those proteins, making the egg wash thinner and more fluid after a few minutes. It glides over the pastry more smoothly, leaving a light, even coating rather than stringy puddles.

The egg itself is what gives pastry its golden color and glossy sheen. Salt doesn’t make the crust magically browner; it simply helps the egg wash do its job better. The result is a more consistent finish, particularly around the edges and decorative details where egg wash tends to collect.

Industry observers note that A pinch of salt won’t turn a lopsided pie into a masterpiece, but it can help a well-made crust look its best. And after we’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time weaving strips of pastry into a lattice for a Thanksgiving pie, I think we’re entitled to a little help with the finishing touches.

BA's Best Lasagna
