⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This lasagna recipe has “rainy Sunday cooking project” written all over it.
  • The secret weapon is the meat sauce.
  • One step you can skip: boiling the noodles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This lasagna recipe has “rainy Sunday cooking project” written all over it. Layers of slow-cooked pork-and-beef ragù, silky Parmesan béchamel, and pasta bake into a rich, creamy lasagna Bolognese with a browned top and crisp edges. Make the sauces ahead to break up the work, or settle in for a day of very good kitchen smells.

The secret weapon is the meat sauce. Why make meatballs only to break them apart? Searing the meat in large balls leaves room for moisture to escape, so you get deep browning instead of a potful of steam. After a long, gentle braise, a potato masher turns them into ragù. Whole canned tomatoes, crushed by hand, give you control over the sauce’s chunky texture.

One step you can skip: boiling the noodles. In side-by-side retests, regular dried lasagna noodles (not no-boil!) produced similar results whether parboiled or layered straight from the box. The ragù and béchamel provide enough moisture to cook the pasta in the oven—as long as every noodle is covered. Spread the sauces to the edges, leaving no dry patches, and making sure the sauce totally covers the top layer of noodles before baking. Round it out with homemade garlic bread and a Caesar salad.

Do I need to buy no-boil lasagna noodles?

Sources indicate that no—use regular dried lasagna noodles, preferably De Cecco. Skipping the boiling step isn’t the same as using noodles labeled “no-boil.” In our original tests, those absorbed too much sauce, leaving the finished lasagna drier than we wanted.

De Cecco Lasagne No.1 Pasta, 16-oz.

Why doesn’t this lasagna have ricotta or mozzarella?

In a recent development, this is a lasagna Bolognese, built around meat ragù and Parmesan-enriched béchamel rather than a separate cheese filling. The béchamel supplies the creaminess, while Parmesan brings salty, nutty flavor. For a less involved version with a cheese filling, try our Cottage Cheese Lasagna.

What’s the best way to split up the work?

In a recent development, make the ragù one day, then tackle the béchamel, assembly, and baking the next. For an even lighter second day, make both sauces ahead and refrigerate them separately; rewarm the béchamel just enough to loosen it before layering. The ragù can be refrigerated for up to 4 days or frozen for up to 3 months, while the béchamel can be refrigerated for 1 day.

Watch Chris make BA’s Best Lasagna.

In a recent development, save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app.

Saving this cooking project for another day? We tasted nine brands to find the best frozen lasagna.

Sources indicate that preheat oven to 225°. Mix 2 lb. ground pork and 1 lb. ground beef chuck (20% fat) with your hands in a large bowl; season generously with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, then mix again. Form into about 18 large meatballs (they don’t need to be perfect—you’ll be mashing them later).

Recent findings suggest that warm 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in 2 batches, cook meatballs, turning occasionally and reducing heat if bottom of pot looks in danger of scorching, until browned all over, about 6 minutes per batch. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet as they’re done.

Reduce heat to medium. Add 2 oz. pancetta (Italian bacon) or slab bacon, chopped, to pot and cook, stirring often, until lightly browned and beginning to crisp, about 5 minutes. Add 1 medium onion, finely chopped, 1 celery stalk, finely chopped, 1 medium carrot, peeled, finely chopped, and 6 garlic cloves, sliced, and cook, stirring occasionally, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until paste is darkened in color, about 2 minutes.

Add ¾ cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until almost completely evaporated, about 5 minutes. Add one 28-oz. can whole peeled tomatoes, crushing with your hands, and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, stirring occasionally, until liquid is jammy and reduced by about half, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth and 1 cup whole milk, then return meatballs to pot. Bring to a simmer. Cover pot partially with a lid, transfer to oven, and cook, checking every hour or so to ensure liquid is at a low simmer and adjusting oven temperature as needed, until meatballs are falling-apart tender, 3–4 hours.

It has been revealed that using a potato masher, break meatballs apart and incorporate into liquid (you should have about 8 cups ragù; transfer pot to stovetop and simmer gently to reduce if needed). Taste and season with more salt and black pepper if needed.

Industry observers note that do ahead: Ragù can be made 4 days ahead. Let cool; cover and chill, or freeze up to 3 months.

Melt 7 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in ¼ cup plus 3 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and cook, whisking occasionally, until mixture smells slightly nutty, about 4 minutes. Whisking constantly, add 6 cups whole milk. Increase heat to medium-high and continue whisking until mixture comes to a simmer. Reduce heat to maintain a simmer and cook, whisking occasionally, until béchamel thickens, about 4 minutes. Continue cooking, whisking occasionally and adjusting heat as needed to maintain a gentle simmer, until béchamel is smooth and velvety, 8–10 minutes more. Remove from heat and whisk in 4 oz. Parmesan cheese, coarsely grated (about 1 cup), a pinch of cayenne pepper, and a pinch of ground nutmeg. (You should have about 6 cups béchamel.) Season with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Transfer to a large bowl and press plastic wrap directly onto surface; let cool slightly.

In a recent development, note: You can skip the following boiling step (and save yourself a pot to wash!). In side-by-side retests, the BA Test Kitchen found that regular dried lasagna noodles (not no-boil) produced similar results whether parboiled or layered straight from the box. To use them uncooked, spread the ragù and béchamel all the way to the edges, covering every noodle completely, and make sure the sauce blankets the top layer of noodles before baking.

If parboiling: Cook 1¼ lb. dried lasagna noodles in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally and separating them so they don’t stick together, until just starting to soften but still snap in half rather than bend when folded; 3 minutes is the magic number. The noodles will be so firm it will just seem all wrong. Using tongs, transfer noodles to a large bowl of cold water to cool. Drain and lay flat in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet, separated by parchment or wax paper.

Industry observers note that lightly coat a 13x9", 4–6-qt. glass or ceramic baking dish with extra-virgin olive oil. Spread 1½ cups ragù in dish. Lay a single layer of noodles over ragù (cut or break noodles as needed to fill any gaps). Spoon 1¼ cups béchamel over noodles, spreading in an even layer with a small offset spatula. Top béchamel with 1½ cups of meat sauce. Repeat layering noodles, béchamel, and ragù 3 more times. Top with a fifth layer of noodles and the remaining 1 cup béchamel.

In a recent development, note: For more pasta in every bite, build six layers instead of five. Start with the same 1½ cups ragù on the bottom of the dish, but use 1 cup béchamel and 1¼ cups ragù between the pasta layers. Finish with a sixth layer of pasta and the remaining 1 cup béchamel.

It has been revealed that cover with a lightly oiled piece of aluminum foil and set lasagna pan on a rimmed baking sheet (just to catch drips). Bake lasagna until bubbling gently around the edges, about 1 hour. Remove from oven. Increase oven temperature to 425° and carefully place rack in top of oven. Remove foil from lasagna and continue to bake until top is browned and crisp around the edges, 10–15 minutes longer. Let sit 10 minutes before serving.

Do ahead: Béchamel can be made 1 day ahead; keep chilled. Rewarm just enough to loosen before using. Lasagna can be assembled 1 month ahead; let cool, then cover with plastic and freeze. Let frozen lasagna thaw overnight in fridge before baking.

Recent findings suggest that editor’s note: This recipe first appeared in our February 2018 issue as part of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen’s definitive takes on iconic dishes. It has been updated with clearer assembly instructions and guidance from additional BA Test Kitchen testing, including the option to skip parboiling regular dried lasagna noodles. Ciara has one request for whoever’s in charge of Christmas dinner: Please, whatever you do, make sure you’re up for the assignment. She’s willing to embrace a little holiday mess, but apparently, there’s a limit to how far that generosity extends into the kitchen.

“All I know is you better not burn no turkey. That’s a culinary crime,” the Grammy-winning singer told Delish. And if you're cooking without a backup bird? You might want to pay especially close attention to that oven. “You better get it right on the first try.”.

According to recent reports, ciara, a mom of four, certainly understands how swiftly the festivities can get away from you. “Christmas in our house is full of love, excitement and a little chaos,” she remarked in a statement. But when it comes to the actual Christmas menu, she’s got some traditions she’s pretty attached to, many of which go all the way back to her childhood in Atlanta, Georgia.

"If you know one thing about us ATLians, you have Thanksgiving on Christmas. The same meal comes back around again," she told Delish.

And we’re talking a serious Southern spread: turkey legs, mac and cheese, candied yams, collard greens, chitlins, and pig feet. She's no longer making pig feet these days, but the other familiar favorites have stuck around. Ciara states those dishes still “make me very happy,” which is as good a reason as any to keep a family tradition going.

Personally, I think we’ve been limiting Thanksgiving dinner to one holiday for far too long.

Tech Report: NASA's Voyager 1 mission forever changed our view of Jupiter

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this Wednesday (Nov.
  • While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune.
  • In a recent development, one of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone. NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.

While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.

In a recent development, one of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter. From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.

Industry observers note that voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.

Recent findings suggest that voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes, which rolled out half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

Just before making its closest approach to the planet, Voyager spotted something remarkable: Jupiter had a thin, faint ring system. Made primarily of dust, the rings appeared only when Voyager saw Jupiter backlit by the sun. No telescope had ever seen this before, but ground-based observatories soon confirmed the rings' existence, and Voyager 2 took even clearer pictures of the rings when it reached Jupiter in July 1979.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring of dust around Jupiter when it was backlit by the sun.

Sources indicate that we now know that all four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — have rings. Today, scientists suspect Jupiter's dusty rings are replenished partially by volcanic eruptions on the planet's volatile moon Io.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This discovery, too, can be linked to Voyager. While making a close approach to Io, the spacecraft witnessed the first-ever volcanic eruption on a world beyond Earth. This observation indicated that moons, not just planets, can be geologically active. In this image, a giant volcano called Loki Patera (the largest volcano on Io, measuring an estimated 125 miles, or 200 km, wide) spews its guts into space.

Voyager 1 witnessed a volcanic eruption (blue) on Io — the first volcaic eruption seen beyond Earth.

Industry observers note that taken together, these observations of Jupiter and its moons highlighted the largest planet and its moons to be a far more dynamic, complicated and chaotic system than anyone had realized. Moreover, the close-up views of these distant worlds made them more than just dots in the sky. It made them fully realized worlds — places to explore, map and eventually visit. Just this week, China's space agency confirmed its intention to send a lander to Jupiter's moon Callisto in the first-ever landing mission to the Jovian system.

Recent findings suggest that voyager 1's work continues in interstellar space, which it officially reached in 2012. With its camera off, it studies the radiation environment of space using magnetic field and plasma detectors — the last two of its 10 science instruments still receiving power. Scientists suspect the legendary probe will fully run out of power in the 2030s.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1218 w)

This Is What Was on the Menu at the First Thanksgiving in 1621

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1218 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Somehow, turkey has spent the last four centuries getting all the glory.
  • Recent findings suggest that for a meal that has been discussed, depicted and reenacted for more than four centuries, the first Thanksgiving has left us surprisingly few details about what anyone actually ate.
  • In a recent development, the gathering took place in Plymouth in the fall of 1621, when about 50 English colonists celebrated their first successful harvest alongside 90 Wampanoag, including their leader, Ousamequin, better known to history as Massasoit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Somehow, turkey has spent the last four centuries getting all the glory.

Recent findings suggest that for a meal that has been discussed, depicted and reenacted for more than four centuries, the first Thanksgiving has left us surprisingly few details about what anyone actually ate. We know there were roughly 140 people, three days of feasting and exactly five deer. Beyond that, the historical record is rather unhelpful. Apparently, nobody thought to write down the menu.

In a recent development, the gathering took place in Plymouth in the fall of 1621, when about 50 English colonists celebrated their first successful harvest alongside 90 Wampanoag, including their leader, Ousamequin, better known to history as Massasoit. It was a meeting between two communities whose relationship was far more complicated than the cheerful scene that would eventually find its way into American classrooms. Although they had formed an alliance earlier that year, cultural differences and tensions of an English settlement on Wampanoag land were hardly going to disappear over dinner.

Industry observers note that and while the English had much to celebrate in bringing in their first harvest, they owed a great deal of that success to Indigenous knowledge. The Wampanoag understood the region’s growing seasons, its waterways and the foods that could be grown and gathered in the surrounding landscape. Their traditions had helped sustain communities there long before the colonists arrived.

The two surviving English accounts of the gathering offer only a few details about the feast itself, but taken together with what historians know about the food traditions of both communities, they give us a rather interesting picture of what may have been on the table.

It has been revealed that edward Winslow, one of the English colonists who attended the gathering, recorded that the Wampanoag went hunting and returned with five deer, which they presented to the colony’s leaders. It’s one of the few specific foods mentioned in his account and an especially substantial contribution to a celebration that lasted three days.

Deer were an important source of food for the Wampanoag, who also made use of their hides, bones and other materials. In England, however, deer hunting was largely reserved for the wealthy, making venison something most ordinary people rarely got to enjoy. The meat may have been roasted over a fire or simmered in a hearty venison stew, although Winslow neglected to tell us how it was prepared. We know exactly how many deer arrived, but what became of them in the kitchen remains a mystery.

Industry observers note that roast turkey has become so thoroughly associated with Thanksgiving that it’s difficult to imagine the holiday without one occupying the center of the table. The trouble is, we don’t actually know whether turkey was served at the original celebration.

Sources indicate that winslow wrote that four Englishmen went hunting for wildfowl and returned with enough to feed the colonists for nearly a week. What he didn’t do was tell us which birds they shot. Wild turkeys were present in the region, but so were ducks, geese and other game birds, all perfectly suitable for roasting over a fire. There’s every possibility that turkey was on the menu, but nothing to suggest it enjoyed the distinction we’ve since bestowed upon it. For all we know, the centerpiece was a duck, and we’ve spent the last few centuries giving credit to the wrong bird.

Corn was one of the most important foods available to both communities, although the English were relatively newly introduced to growing it. The Wampanoag had cultivated maize for generations, developing agricultural practices suited to the region’s soil and growing seasons. Their knowledge was enormously valuable to the colonists, whose first attempts at establishing a food supply had been anything but fruitful.

In a recent development, one traditional Wampanoag preparation was nasaump, a thick porridge made from ground corn, sometimes cooked with other ingredients. Corn could also be ground into meal for simple breads, early relatives of the cornbread we bake today, or used to thicken stews and make other hearty dishes.

The waters around Plymouth were full of food, provided you knew where to look and how to catch it. The Wampanoag had long fished the region’s rivers and coastline, gathering shellfish and catching everything from bass and cod to eels. Clams, mussels and lobsters were plentiful too.

Sources indicate that the English were beginning to take advantage of these resources by 1621. William Bradford, the Plymouth colony’s governor, wrote of the colonists catching substantial quantities of cod and bass during the summer. A freshly caught fish could be roasted or boiled, while clams and mussels might be cooked over a fire. Lobster was another plentiful local catch that was enjoyed regularly. The variety of ocean fare available might have made for a Thanksgiving spread that looked rather more like a seafood boil than the feast we know today.

Industry observers note that squash and pumpkin were crucial crops in Wampanoag agriculture, and their ability to keep well after harvest made them especially useful as the colder weather set in. Both could be roasted, boiled or added to stews, much like we still prepare winter squash today, though without the benefit of a balsamic glaze.

The English called pumpkins pompions, a name I think we abandoned prematurely. They were familiar with the vegetable, although the varieties growing in Latest England differed from those they might have seen at home. A pumpkin dish would have been entirely plausible at the harvest celebration, but anyone hoping for a slice of pumpkin pie would have to wait almost two centuries. The colonists had limited supplies of wheat flour, butter and sugar, and the familiar custard-filled pie wouldn’t appear in American cookbooks until 1796.

According to recent reports, the Wampanoag grew beans alongside corn and squash, three crops that complemented each other remarkably well. Cornstalks supported climbing beans, while squash vines spread across the ground and helped shade the soil. The combination was as useful in the garden as it was on the plate.

Recent findings suggest that A traditional Wampanoag stew called sobaheg combines ingredients like corn, beans, squash and meat or fish, depending on what’s available or in season. The combination of corn and beans also appears in succotash, another dish with Indigenous Fresh England roots that remains an American favorite.

Recent findings suggest that the forests and wetlands of Fresh England offered plenty beyond cultivated crops. Chestnuts, walnuts, hazelnuts, acorns, wild grapes and cranberries were among the foods the Wampanoag knew how to gather and prepare, each with its own season and uses.

According to recent reports, nuts could be eaten plain, stored or ground into meal, while fruits could be enjoyed fresh or preserved for later. Acorns required particular attention, since their natural bitterness had to be leached out with water before they could be used in cooking. It’s one of the few ingredients we’ve more or less surrendered entirely to the squirrels.

In a recent development, of all the wild fruits available, cranberries have perhaps the most recognizable place on a modern Thanksgiving table. Their natural tartness eventually found a friend in sugar, giving rise to the cranberry sauce that’s become nearly as much a part of the holiday as the turkey itself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Food writer Rachel Gurjar made this goat kari for her “lifelong idol” Madhur Jaffrey, the renowned Indian cookbook author, at a dinner Gurjar hosted in her Brooklyn apartment in September 2022. When Jaffrey asked for the recipe, Gurjar knew she had to include it in her debut cookbook, East to East.

Sources indicate that you can find goat meat at your local halal butcher or substitute lamb. If opting for goat, Gurjar recommends requesting a bone-in “curry cut,” which means the butcher will cut the meat into 2- to 3-inch pieces that are ideal for braising.

Industry observers note that while you can use store-bought garam masala, Gurjar always DIYs her own spice blend inspired by the one her mother used to make back in India. “It’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional,” she writes. “This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again.” You can also customize your blend: Add more cinnamon and fennel for a sweeter garam masala, or up the black pepper and cloves for a spicier kick.

Featured in “Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in Fresh York City.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sometimes, all there's time for on Thanksgiving is buying a store-bought pumpkin pie.
  • Planning, shopping and preparing a full Thanksgiving dinner is a Herculean task for even the most experienced home cook.
  • In a recent development, I recently drove around town and picked up pies from six major grocery store chains so I could conduct an official taste test before the big day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Sometimes, all there's time for on Thanksgiving is buying a store-bought pumpkin pie. I tested six to find out which one tasted the most homemade.

Planning, shopping and preparing a full Thanksgiving dinner is a Herculean task for even the most experienced home cook. There are many moving parts, and it can certainly be overwhelming when there is a houseful of hungry guests ready to dive into the biggest family meal of the year. That’s why I think there is no shame in turning to store-bought options for some elements of the meal. If baking isn’t your forte, but you still want to offer a traditional pumpkin pie for dessert, stores across the country are ready to help.

In a recent development, I recently drove around town and picked up pies from six major grocery store chains so I could conduct an official taste test before the big day. The contenders are:.

I sampled and ranked each one based on overall appearance, the flavor and texture of the crust, and, finally, the consistency of the filling and spices used. I was certainly surprised by my top choice.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Coming in at the bottom of my ranked list is the Bakeshop pumpkin pie from Aldi. This 8-inch pie is 1-1/2 pounds and costs $5.29. Before cutting a slice, I noticed that the crust on this pie was quite pale. So much so, I even checked the label to make sure I wasn’t expected to bake it before serving. When I took a bite, the taste was what I would expect from an undercooked crust. It was gummy and almost tasted raw. The filling was quite sweet, with the sugar, brown sugar and molasses flavors being the most prevalent and the pumpkin pie spices taking a backseat.

Bottom Line: The pumpkin pie from Aldi is a bargain at only $5.29, but the undercooked, super-sweet filling didn’t impress.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Selling for a bargain at $4.94, the pumpkin pie from Walmart was the least expensive pie I sampled. This 8-inch pie is 1 pound, 6 ounces. You might notice from the photograph that with this pie, the crust separated from the filling after cutting a slice. Sometimes this occurs when the custard is overcooked. Once again, I wasn’t impressed with the color of the crust and hoped for more browning and flavor. The filling also had a similar overly sweet taste that I noticed in the Aldi pie. I wish the spices in this pie were kicked up a notch or two as well.

Bottom Line: The price of a Walmart pumpkin pie can’t be beat, but the dessert isn’t the most flavorful of those I tested. Next time I might jazz it up with some spiced pecans just before serving.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, the pumpkin pie from Trader Joe’s was quite different from all the other pies in this sample group. Right out of the box, I noticed both the crust and the filling were a deep brown color. Quite a departure from some of the other anemic-looking pies. Selling for $6.99, this 9-inch pie is larger and heavier at 1 pound, 9.4 ounces. Reading the ingredient list, this pie included cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, cloves and allspice. As someone who loves these flavors, I couldn’t wait to dive in.

This pie definitely didn’t hold back. The flavors are very bold, and the crust is well-browned. However, these spices are so bold that you almost lose the pumpkin’s flavor. This pie might have benefited from pulling back slightly on the spices to further highlight the star of the show, aka the pumpkin.

Recent findings suggest that bottom Line: If you like very bold pumpkin pie spices, this dessert from Trader Joe’s will fit the bill. However, the strong flavor might be divisive around the dinner table.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Marie Callender’s is a brand known for pies, and you can pick up an unbaked pie in the freezer section of many grocery stores for a budget-friendly $5.97. It weighs 2 pounds, 4 ounces, and measures 8-1/2 inches across. There are both benefits and drawbacks to purchasing an unbaked pie. Since it’s kept frozen, there’s no need for a bunch of preservatives and fillers used in some of the shelf-stable pies I picked up at other stores. However, when you have to bake the pie yourself, there is room for user error and a risk of an overbaked or underbaked dessert.

In terms of flavor and texture, this pie was middle-of-the-road across the board. The crust was good, it just wasn’t a showstopper that I’d be excited to bring to the table. I appreciated the creamy filling, but once again, I just wanted a more pumpkin-forward flavor.

Bottom Line: The flavor and texture of the Marie Callender’s crust was delightful, but it was not as visually appealing as some other store-bought options.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Industry observers note that at almost 2-1/2 pounds and 10 inches in diameter, the $7.99 pumpkin pie from Kroger (Mariano’s in my neck of the woods) was the largest of the pumpkin pies in this taste test. In addition, the perfectly fluted crust on this pie was lovely. It looked homemade and baked to perfection. The most prevalent flavor in the filling is cinnamon, with nutmeg, allspice and ginger lingering in the background. The pie cut well and sat nicely on the serving plate, but had a slightly gelatinous texture rather than a rich, creamy custard consistency. I would certainly buy this pie again, but next time I think I would kick it up a notch by serving with a bourbon whipped cream to really wow my guests.

Bottom Line: This was the most visually impressive pumpkin pie on the list and one that I’d be proud to present at the dessert table.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

According to recent reports, the pumpkin pie at my local Albertson’s (we call it Jewel in the Chicago area) is just shy of 8 inches wide and weighs 1 pound, 4 ounces for $7.99. Ultimately, in this taste test, this pie came closer to tasting homemade than any other option. This was the only pie I found that struck the ideal balance between warm fall spices and signature pumpkin flavor. I loved the prevalent cinnamon notes and the velvety texture of the filling. The crust was attractively presented and perfectly baked. It was actually the smallest of the pies I sampled and on the higher end in terms of price, but every bite was worth it.

Bottom Line: If I’m not making a homemade pumpkin pie this year, I’ll be relying on Albertson’s to do the work for me!

Sources indicate that which store-bought pie is your fave? Let us know in the comments below!

Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday.
  • President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.
  • Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.

Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.

Much of the hearing focused on Carr and his threats to use the FCC to punish broadcasters he disagrees with.

Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., said that he expects Carr will not last long in his position once Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.

“Mr. Carr, if you're listening now, know you're going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions … so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place,” Luján said.

According to recent reports, the nomination of Thumann Severs, who currently serves as senior counsel to Carr, has led to consternation among Democrats due to continued vacancies at the FCC. The five-member commission is intended to have three members of the president’s party, including the chair, and two in the minority.

Recent findings suggest that currently Carr serves alongside fellow Republican Olivia Trusty and Democrat Anna M. Gomez, whose term expired earlier this year. Gomez may continue to serve through next year under the law if a replacement is not nominated and confirmed.

Democrats are concerned that if Thumann Severs were to be confirmed, the commission’s three Republican members could constitute a quorum on their own, allowing Trump to fire Gomez.

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., stated Senate precedent is to move pairs of one Democratic and one Republican nominee for the FCC and that he “strongly” believed the Thumann Severs nomination should have been paired with a renomination of Gomez in order to continue having “both parties at the table.”.

“A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation [and] I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press [that] serves everyone,” Hickenlooper remarked.

In addition to urging Trump to renominate Gomez, Democrats underlined the need for a second Democratic member of the commission.

Hickenlooper highlighted Thumann Severs’ close work with Carr, who Democrats and some Republicans have been critical of for comments about using the FCC’s public interest standard against television stations airing programming Carr disagrees with.

Thumann Severs’ work at the FCC currently focuses on the Wireline, Public Safety and Homeland Security, and Consumer and Governmental Affairs bureaus, rather than the Media Bureau.

Recent findings suggest that committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has also been critical of Carr’s comments. On Tuesday, he listed the FCC’s request for ABC-owned stations to submit early license renewals alongside earlier incidents in which he stated Democrats encouraged the weaponization of the FCC against conservative voices.

“The First Amendment places key limits on the government’s ability to regulate speech,” Cruz stated. “The FCC possesses significant regulatory authority over communications, so there is always a risk that it could weaponize its authority against Americans with whom it disagrees.”.

Thumann Severs committed to Cruz that she would base licensing decisions on “the law and the record” and not use the FCC’s authority to “pressure or punish” broadcasters for protected speech.

However, when Sen. Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., questioned Thumann Severs on whether the FCC could punish broadcasters the president disagreed with, Thumann Severs repeated one of Carr’s arguments in discussing the FCC’s role.

“Broadcasters are subject to public interest obligations as part of the public trustee model in exchange for the licenses that they hold,” she said. “As part of those public interest obligations, they are subject to many different rules and requirements, and the FCC is charged with enforcing and investigating the public interest standard against broadcasters.”.

Under repeated questions from Markey about Carr’s previous remarks, Thumann Severs said she would base her decisions “in the facts and the law and the record.”.

Sources indicate that luján also asked Thumann Severs to name problems where she had disagreed with Carr or Trump. While she stated her decisions would be her own, she declined to name any examples of disagreement.

In addition to questions about Carr, Democrats asked the nominee about the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides low-cost connectivity for schools and libraries, and the Universal Service Fund, which funds the E-Rate program and other programs.

Thumann Severs noted that she believes the E-Rate program has been successful and that the FCC has a statutory obligation to provide some kind of discounted service to schools and libraries. But she was less forthcoming on whether the FCC could shut down the program as it currently exists without congressional approval or whether the program should be restricted only to rural areas.

Late last month, Democratic members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, led by Communications and Technology Subcommittee ranking member Doris Matsui, D-Calif., sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Cruz urging Gomez’s renomination with any move to confirm a Republican nominee.

According to recent reports, “Commissioner Gomez has shown the experience and judgment to continue that work,” the members wrote. “We therefore ask that the Senate pair any fresh Republican nominee with her renomination to a full term, consistent with the bipartisan design Congress built into this agency.”.

On Monday, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights also sent a letter to committee leadership urging a delay on the hearing and any vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination until Gomez can be renominated.

“Independent agencies should not be extensions of presidential will: their leaders should exercise independent judgement based on their expertise and statutory mandates,” the group wrote.

Cruz did not indicate Tuesday when the committee might vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination, and no markup has yet been announced by the committee of hers' and those of three others for two posts at NASA and one at the Transportation Department who also testified.

Recent findings suggest that delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Whether it was roasting a chicken, pouring an outrageously large Cosmopolitan, or just organizing her pantry, I’d happily watch Ina Garten do just about anything on television. But there’s apparently one TV gig that even the Barefoot Contessa can't stomach, and I’m a little devastated we’ll never get to see it.

During the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, Garten got to talking with guest Rose Byrne about opportunities that felt too intimidating to pursue. Ina didn’t have to think very hard to come up with her own example.

It has been revealed that “Somebody asked me to do Dancing with the Stars,” she revealed. “I thought, ‘Nobody needs to see that. That’s not happening.’”.

With which I respectfully disagree. I think quite a few of us would happily clear our schedules to see Ina Garten attempt a salsa. Unfortunately, Garten wasn’t particularly eager to find out how she'd fare in the ballroom. “The closer I got to the day when I had to do it, the more I’d have nightmares,” she admitted.

Byrne was sympathetic, acknowledging that she’d be terrified of competing, too.

Still, this is a woman who’s made some pretty bold decisions throughout her career. Garten left her job working on nuclear energy policy in Washington, D.C., to buy a specialty food store in the Hamptons with virtually no experience running one. There were some early mishaps, including a batch of roast chickens nobody wanted until she changed how they were displayed, and those experiences eventually helped shape the approachable cooking philosophy behind her hugely successful cookbooks.

Sources indicate that and Garten has certainly gotten comfortable sharing the spotlight over the years. In Delish’s recent interview with Garten and Jennifer Garner, the longtime friends traded stories about their kitchen adventures, favorite recipes, and even late-night In-N-Out Burger runs. Give Ina some good food and someone she loves spending time with, and she's in her element.

It has been revealed that personally, though, I can't stop imagining Jeffrey in the audience holding up a giant “10” sign in support of his wife. We really missed out on something special.

#123066. Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in Newly introduced York City

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1265 w)

Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in Newly introduced York City

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit.
  • As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood.
  • In a recent development, in many ways, this transition is happening outside of me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit. It is a small but enduring presence, tended to around the clock, its care passed from one person to the next so that the light never goes out. I’ve often thought about how much of life is like this, how we are constantly passing the torch from one version of ourselves to another.

As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood. I was becoming someone different from the girl I had been, carrying parts of her with me but beginning to understand the world through a fresh lens. Now, years later, I find myself at another such transition: I am becoming a different version of a woman, one I am still getting to know.

In a recent development, in many ways, this transition is happening outside of me. Thirteen years ago, I moved away from my family in Mumbai and the home where Diwali had always been celebrated. For all those years, the rituals continued, even as I participated in them from thousands of miles away, mostly over video calls. Back in Mumbai, Diwali meant a house full of family and friends, kitchens bustling with cooking and frying, and the warm glow of diyas illuminating the mandir. I was no longer physically there, but I remained part of it. This year, for the first time, I hosted my parents for Diwali in the home I’ve built for myself in New York City.

According to recent reports, it felt cataclysmic, or at least I was making it feel that way in my head. As I welcomed a different version of myself, I was also taking on a latest role within my family. I was no longer simply the daughter returning to their house for Diwali; I was the one opening my home, preparing the food, tending to the rituals, and making space for the people who first taught me what this celebration means. There is perhaps no greater joy than watching the people I love receive and experience care. And yet, this was a responsibility I had chosen to take on, and one that felt particularly daunting as the eldest daughter. I wanted to get it right.

It has been revealed that for me, that care has always found its way to the table. Food is how my family celebrates, how we mark occasions, and, perhaps most importantly, how we look after one another. So naturally, much of my energy went into planning the meal. Despite my best efforts, my dad promptly assigned himself the task of making the goat kari—apparently, even after 13 years away, some things hadn’t changed. We headed to our local butcher in Brooklyn to buy fresh goat meat, and almost immediately, his attention turned to the spice tolerance of my guests.

Sources indicate that “How much spice can your friends tolerate?” he kept asking me. “Should I keep it at a level six? But our level six might be their level ten. What do I do?” he lamented. “Relax, they’ll be able to handle it! Just make it our level five,” I told him.

Recent findings suggest that I gave in and handed over part of the kitchen to my mother, too. She took charge of the paneer, cooking generous chunks in a luscious onion-tomato gravy and making the chapatis. Selfishly, I didn’t mind relinquishing that responsibility: This would be my one chance for the year to eat chapatis fresh off the tava, puffed up and piping hot, and made by my mother.

As the days drew closer, I found myself loosening my grip on the intends I’d made. My parents had their own ideas about what needed to be cooked, and while I was initially resistant to them taking over (any immigrant will tell you how hard it is to get our parents to just relax!), I was learning that hosting didn’t necessarily mean doing everything myself. It also meant making room for everyone to contribute and allowing new rituals to form.

It has been revealed that the evening began with freshly fried moong vadas. My mother, of course, insisted on frying them for everyone, right before serving. Made from soaked and ground mung lentils, these little fritters are crisp and golden on the outside, with a soft, almost creamy interior. They have a naturally earthy, nutty flavor from the lentils, sharpened with green chiles, ginger, and spices.

Moong vadas are best eaten immediately, still hot out of the oil, with a tangy green chutney. The scene reminded me of Diwalis back in Mumbai, when the vadas rarely even made it to the serving platter: Everyone would gather around the kitchen, waiting for the next batch to come out of the kadai, reaching for them before they had a chance to cool. I saw the same thing happening in my kitchen in Latest York.

In a recent development, in the meantime, my friends Leanne and Christina took charge of the tamarind margaritas, my ode to the soft, sweet-tart tamarind candies I grew up savoring as a kid. The tangy cocktails were a welcome counterpoint to the savory fritters, the perfect way to wake up our taste buds (and made exercising some restraint with those moong vadas before dinner particularly difficult). My brother helped set the table and move furniture around, just as we used to do for our parents back in Mumbai. There was something deeply comforting about watching us fall into these old rhythms.

The table eventually came together with a mix of dishes that felt both familiar and celebratory. There was chana masala from my cookbook, East to East, alongside my dad’s goat kari, slow-cooked with spices until the meat was tender. My mother’s saucy tomato-onion paneer was accompanied by a pile of chapatis that disappeared almost as promptly as they came off the stove. We served everything family-style, laying out the dishes on kansa thalis, traditional Indian plates made from bronze or bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. They reminded me of the way my grandparents served meals, and I wanted to bring a little of that into our Diwali celebration.

Recent findings suggest that at the center of the spread was a vegetable pulao, fragrant basmati rice cooked with carrots, cabbage, cauliflower, and whole spices. Alongside it, I placed bowls of pickled onions and mango achaar, whose sharp, tangy bite cuts through the richness of the karis. There was also cucumber raita, cool and creamy, offering a welcome respite from the heat of the spices. These accompaniments might seem like small additions, but they are essential to the balance of an Indian meal. Every bite can be a little different, depending on what you bring together on your plate.

For dessert, I made homemade gulab jamun, my brother’s favorite. The soft dumplings are made from milk solids and fried until golden, then soaked in a warm saffron-and-cardamom-scented sugar syrup.

Industry observers note that as I sat cuddled among both my families, I realized that while it wasn’t the perfectly orchestrated dinner I’d imagined when I first started planning, it was something better. The family I was born into celebrating Diwali alongside the family I’d chosen and built in New York, all gathered around the same table and enjoying every minute of it. Perhaps keeping the flame alive was never about re-creating the past exactly as it was but about allowing it to illuminate whatever comes next.

#123064. A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1878 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Saveur ↗ Open Full Page

A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that on a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo.
  • Industry observers note that on the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge.
  • Bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo. Six lanes of traffic jockeyed inches from her left shoulder, while the black waters of the Río Ozama coursed below. “Oh my God, Oli, what are we doing?” she remarked. “Nobody does this.” Evangelista is the communications manager for Santo Domingo’s most intriguing restaurant, Casarré. Her boss, Swiss Dominican chef Olivier Bur, was leading Evangelista, photographer Clay Williams, and me beyond the fortified walls of the Zona Colonial, where few travel on foot.

Industry observers note that on the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge. Live bachata drowned out the traffic overhead. Bur procured a substantial bottle of Presidente and plastic cups from a vendor, poured, and raised a “Salud!”.

Bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere. Moving slowly, he’s learned the textures of the city. Still, for the next six days, he took Williams and me to his most beloved restaurants by car. We visited a string of chimi stands where hawkers compete for clientele through the night; a chicharrón spot where couples dance shoeless on the cool tile floor; and a cafeteria where boys shuffle stewed eggplant, beets, and goat to bus drivers en route. Places like these are the “infrastructure for life,” Bur said. “Thirty years ago, there was nothing else.”.

According to recent reports, over the last couple of decades, however, another dining scene has sprouted. Dominican chefs have returned from kitchens in Mexico, Japan, or Switzerland to explore the forgotten and sometimes shunned ingredients of their (or their parents’) homes. They served us conch, cassava, breadfruit, and djon-djon mushrooms in sashimis, foams, tostones, and surprising dessert creams. The dishes were fresh and exciting, but local and global traditions have always mingled—as such, the cuisine is not “Fresh Dominican,” it’s simply “Dominican,” fully expressed.

Calle Andrés Julio Aybar 13+1 829 545 7503.

In a recent development, the Piantini neighborhood was once verdant and sleepy, according to Bur. Now it’s a bustling business district. Most of the remaining vegetation decorates the façades of restaurants, like Ajualä’s. Brushed palm thatch and a bushy barba de Fidel (Fidel’s beard) tree greet you at the tall aged-steel door.

Venezuelan chef Saverio Stassi is a leader among the culinary latest guard. His treatment of local ingredients is virtuosic. He confits guinea hen in cocoa butter and tops breadfruit tostones with local yellowfin and Cambita avocado; and over two days, his team bathes the succulent goat from the northwest—where they famously graze on wild oregano, self-infusing their meat—in Seville orange juice before roasting it in a barbacoa pit.

Calle Max Henríquez Ureña 14+1 809 547 3592.

Sources indicate that chef Erik Malmsten has cooked at his parents’ cabaret in Gothenburg, Sweden, at Aquavit in New York, and at Bocuse d’Or competitions around the world. But to take his career to the next level, he returned to his mother’s homeland to open a Nordic-Japanese restaurant.

“You’ll see, it’s really good,” Bur told us. The meal starts with “lobster chicharrón,” with a reduced crustacean bisque, fried into airy orange sheets of bubbly crackling and served with tōgarashi Kewpie. Then, a parade of sashimi, like king fish, served with brown butter soy emulsion, ikura, and lemon zest. It ends with Dominican chocolates, molded, painted, and plated to look like koi fish on a synchronized swim.

Calle Caonabo 35+1 809 584 9481.

If, like me, you come from a pizza region, you might not be inclined to use one of your Santo Domingo meal slots on a pie. But I urge you: Make time for Casa Gazcue. Spanish Dominican chef Francis Pena’s 48-hour-fermented crust comes blistered and sometimes covered in honeyed sesame seeds. Iterations are variously laden with spicy Dominican oxtail, chimi sandwich sauce, pistachio, and jamón ibérico, but you don’t have to choose: For groups, he serves a rosca (a round with an open middle) of six sections arranged like floral pizza petals.

Calle Pablo Casals+1 809 562 6060.

In 1954, the Bonarelli family opened the legendary Italian restaurant Vesuvio. For decades, it was the place—the only place—to go out for a formal sit-down meal around here. Vesuvio closed over 20 years ago, but the founder’s grandson, Giancarlo Bonarelli, now runs Bottega Fratelli in a sleek modern building in Naco (Piantini’s equally upscale neighbor).

It has been revealed that you’ll notice a great variety of beet dishes in the Dominican Republic. Farmers harvest them year-round in the cool, pine-forested Costanza Valley. Try them here, roasted and served with blue cheese, chèvre, candied nuts, and honey. Also try a carpaccio of king mackerel, caught off the eastern coast, or any of the risottos, an emblem of the family’s enduring Italian culinary influence.

Calle del Seminario #57+1 809 565 1621.

Recent findings suggest that hideyoshi Tateyama’s parents opened Samurai in 1990. The restaurant joined Vesuvio, along with one or two others in that era’s small restaurant scene. It still stands out today among the many dozens.

Sources indicate that be sure to order the guatapaná con coco. A tried-and-true combo of shrimp and coconut imbued with native guatapaná leaf, tobiko, sesame seed, and scallion—it’s been on the menu for two decades. Also, don’t miss the chance to sample a sashimi of the meter-long “calamar diamante” from the Samaná region. It’s simply brightened with lemon zest. Meals are capped with a green tea amaro. Once a month, Tateyama personally runs a chef’s-choice omakase service.

Avenida Independencia 312+1 809 682 1433.

On the day we visited Villar Hermanos, lines formed around the block for each of two buffets. Women balanced towers of takeout containers tightly wrapped in plastic. It was the World Cup Final, and people were rushing to get some of the city’s best comfort food to their coffee tables. “This is the place to come for all the Dominican classics,” Bur told us.

We found a large table under the sprawling canopy of a banyan tree and ordered mofongo. It was moist, punctuated with crisp chicharrón crackling. The sancocho, the classic Domincan stew thick with potato and yuca starch, assumed extra body when alternating spoonfuls of broth and rice. While I didn’t have my coveted mangú and tres golpes (salami, queso frito, and eggs), I would trade my house and car to live next door and eat breakfast there every morning under the filtered sun.

Avenida San Vicente de Paúl, Santo Domingo Este 11504+1 809 244 8906.

On Avenida San Vicente de Paúl in East Santo Domingo, scooters zip down the busy street all through the night, many popping over a curb into the Plaza Del Chimi. The “plaza” is a stretch of  10 to 15 “chimi” sandwich stalls outfitted with griddles and prep stations heaped with roasted pork shoulders. Dealers swiftly slice the meat, lay it on the griddle, flip it onto a squishy pan de agua roll, and top it with cabbage, tomato, and tangy pink sauce before sliding it into your mitts. The stalls are open till 6 a.m. When they run out of beer, a man runs bottles from a cooler at his house and serves them in paper bags.

Avenida Independencia KM 8+1 809 532 2580.

It has been revealed that across from a shopping mall on Avenida Indepencia, about a dozen cars cram into five parking spaces for the lunch or late-night staple pica pollo. Behind a crowded serving station, a woman slides eight pounds of chicken into a hotel pan, and the picking begins. Six sets of tongs compete for room, like bird beaks, snapping the chicken into styrofoam containers before barely holding them shut with strained rubber bands. Another eight pounds comes out less than two minutes later.

According to recent reports, pica pollo is one of the lasting influences of Chinese immigrants in Santo Domingo. Usually cooks marinate it in bitter orange, garlic, and oregano before coating it in flour and spice (in this case we detected Chinese five-spice) and deep-frying it to golden brown.

Avenida Cayetano Germosén+1 809 286 2141.

At Parque Mirador Sur, teens and whole families perch along concrete walls and hilltops eating fried yuca and succulent mojo-dipped chicharrón with long toothpicks. It comes from the crowded, steel-barred serving window across the street: Chicharrones Light de la Cayetano.

In a recent development, among all the chicharrón we ate in the city (there was a lot), theirs stood out. There’s a small covered seating area where you can order beer to share. Bachata plays loud over a hanging speaker. Women take turns kicking off their heels to do the four-step shimmy with their jevos (boyfriends).

Calle Ciriaco Ramirez 70+1 809 689 5544.

Sources indicate that the Colmado, Bur indicates, “is essential to Dominican life. Everything happens there.” For 70 years, Colmado La Venganza has anchored a prominent corner in the Don Bosco neighborhood. It’s hosted thousands of late-night domino games and sports viewing parties. We were there during the World Cup.

According to recent reports, at the entrance, a man with a crisp-edged haircut, big sunglasses, and a pressed floral shirt parked his shoe on a milk crate while a boy polished it with a rag. Inside, groups spanning all ages gathered at high-tops and around the bar. Folks shared triple-stacked ham, pickle, and cheese sandwiches, pressed, cubed, and spiked with toothpicks: the “sándwich especial.” Leaving the bar, chef Raniel Cruz (part of our party) texted his mom in Montreal. She responded: “Wait, you’re at Venganza? I used to drink there.”.

Calle Luperón 52+1 849 460 5600.

One couldn’t understand the Dominican Republic’s vast culinary splendor in a lifetime, but if you had just one night to try, you’d want to dine at Casarré. Every Tuesday, the team takes excursions. We accompanied them to meet the countryside cooks, who wrap guáyiga root masa in leaves from the almond trees on Najayo beach and bake it in coal-covered pots. We visited a produce market, where vendors passed fruit samples, like little red “frutas milagrosas” that, when chewed beforehand, make bitter limes taste like sweet limeade.

At night, in a candlelit, contemplative room in the Zona Colonial, Bur and his team showcase their findings in a series of sublime, thoughtful dishes. On our visit, they presented djon-djon mushrooms from the Haitian borderlands in a sweet, guáyiga-thickened foam and in the broth of a citrusy okra and fish soup. Chef Isabella Sánchez explained: “The broth is murky, like the current state of the Río Ozama. It represents the negative aspects of our water—contamination and conflict—and the beautiful: the fish, the beaches, and our grandmother’s tea.”.

Avenida Lope de Vega 44+1 809 816 7200.

Recent findings suggest that smoke from an open Uruguayan-style parrilla floats in the soft light over two stories. Our waiter mentioned, “We want this to feel like a Sunday asado.” Indeed, the smoke, the char, and the Malbec are there. This asado, though, also has Negronis smoked tableside and poured from a glass goose. As we awaited a perfect aged rib eye, we enjoyed paper-thin beef carpaccio with foie, and a paella-esque rice with soft leeks, cilantro, and pork trotters.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

Chipotle’s Thanksgiving Eve BOGO Returns For One Night Only—Here's How To Get It

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (365 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanksgiving is practically an Olympic event for eating, but there’s nothing wrong with a little warm-up the night before.
  • The deal runs Wednesday, November 25, from 5 to 9 p.m.
  • But, as expected, there’s some fine print worth reading before you get in line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving is practically an Olympic event for eating, but there’s nothing wrong with a little warm-up the night before. Chipotle is bringing back its Thanksgiving Eve BOGO deal, giving you a perfectly good excuse to grab a burrito with an old friend before the turkey, stuffing, and inevitable food coma take over.

The deal runs Wednesday, November 25, from 5 to 9 p.m. local time at participating U.S. restaurants, with the usual buy one entrée, get one free format we all know and love.

But, as expected, there’s some fine print worth reading before you get in line. You’ll need to be a Chipotle Rewards member, order at the restaurant, and scan your Rewards card at checkout. The free entrée must cost the same as or less than the one you're buying, and you can claim up to five free entrées per check. Kids’ meals don't qualify, and ordering ahead through the app, online, or for delivery won't work.

Sources indicate that the timing has changed a bit from last year, too, when it ran from 4 p.m. all the way until closing. This time, you've got a four-hour window, so make sure that one friend you have who’s perpetually late gets the memo.

According to recent reports, “The response last year indicated us how much our guests embraced the occasion,” Stephanie Perdue, Chipotle's senior vice president of brand marketing, remarked in a statement. According to the chain, the promotion ended up being its biggest sales-driving campaign of 2025, so a return trip was probably inevitable.

It has been revealed that and if you’re stuffed and don’t feel like leaving the couch the next day, there’s a little something for the post-Thanksgiving crowd as well. From Friday, November 27, through Monday, November 30, Chipotle is waiving its delivery fee on eligible orders placed through its app or website with code CYBER26. You’ll need to spend at least $10 in the U.S. or $12 in Canada, and delivery menu prices may be higher, with other fees still applying.

If nothing else, it’s a convenient excuse to take a break from the annual challenge of finding increasingly creative ways to eat leftover turkey.

Breaking: Rift grows among Senate Democrats over who will lead in majority

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin hold a news conference calling for a “bold direction” for Senate Democrats on Tuesday.
  • Industry observers note that more Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E.
  • In a recent development, but Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sens. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin hold a news conference calling for a “bold direction” for Senate Democrats on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Industry observers note that more Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead their conference in the majority.

In a recent development, but Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., publicly calling for a different leader or a “concrete blueprint” that provides change.

According to recent reports, “I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it.”.

Sanders stated during a news conference Tuesday the election was about “change and the need for the Democratic Party to move in a latest and bold direction.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders mentioned, calling for an “economy that works for all, not just the people on top.”.

“Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction?” he asked. “No.”.

Some incoming members and now incumbents have pointed to Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen as one possibility to challenge Schumer. Van Hollen had previously thrown cold water on the idea by saying he was instead “kicking the tires” on a presidential run in 2028 but has recently changed his tune.

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking stated he “has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode.”.

Slotkin did not endorse anyone for leader but said she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen yesterday.

Industry observers note that “Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete proposal that’s definitely different. I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she stated, urging her peers to “withhold quorum” when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections “until you get that plan and you feel like you have a voice in that plan.”.

According to recent reports, she urged not just a roadmap for the first 100 days, but ideas for how to “communicate differently.” As for her own future, she mentioned, “I am not actively seeking this job. I’m seeking change.”.

Asked about his plans Monday evening, Van Hollen mentioned, “It’s not about me, but I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, with a particular ear to new members who have just come off the campaign trail.”.

In a recent development, “What I’ve stated from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about what we're going to do with the power and responsibilities that have been invested in us,” Van Hollen said. “I’m in listening mode and haven’t shut the door.”.

Van Hollen took it a step further at an event Tuesday in Washington, D.C., criticizing the minority leader and Democrats’ campaign arm over their preferences in some primaries. “Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates,” he stated, according to a livestream of the event.

Industry observers note that schumer tried to tamp down the suggestion of a rivalry. “We talk frequently, and we’re united — united in lowering costs, and united in ending this damn war,” he said of Van Hollen.

Others threw their support behind Schumer ahead of the Democratic leadership elections, which are expected to take place in December.

Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., praised Schumer for raising money and recruiting candidates like Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Roy Cooper of North Carolina to help land at minimum seven seats, and potentially nine if Alaska and Mississippi ultimately swing their way.

“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done. And that is why you will see, despite all grumblings, enormous gratitude,” she said.

In a recent development, gillibrand pointed to candidates like Scott Colom, the Democrat in Mississippi who is presently leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a nail-biter of a race. “That wave doesn’t get created by magic. It gets created by hard work and putting the pieces together over years,” she remarked.

Colom, however, has been noncommittal, telling MS NOW, “Too many of our leaders are from the same areas of the country,” pointing to the Brooklyn roots of both Schumer and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to run for speaker on the House side.

Industry observers note that sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., noted he and Schumer have had their differences. But he implied he backs him for majority leader: “At the end of the day, these are historic numbers. It’s time for us to unify. We are going to work together as a caucus to plan together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think we have the person who I think is going to lead us there.”.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., said Democrats have “an opportunity to do things differently, and I think we will, regardless of who the leader is. It doesn’t really matter whose name is on the door.”.

Industry observers note that “Yes,” he noted of his support for Schumer, noting that so far, nobody has officially stepped up to the plate. “This is a guy that worked incredibly hard over the last couple of years. I know people have other opinions about this. But we have a mandate to do things and get things done for the American people.”.

“And we can do that with Chuck Schumer.”.

Mark Schoeff Jr., Paul M. Krawzak and Kelly Livingston contributed to this report.

Sticky Miso Chicken and More Recipes We Made This Week
