In a recent development, adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he introduced Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Open for: Lunch through late night.

It has been revealed that as Jonathan Nunn wrote in his guide to north London’s best-value restaurants, “Durak, a tantuni salonu run by Dogan Yesil on West Green Road, is the superior late night snack template.” Only the tantuni, a speciality which originates in the city of Mersin on the southern coast of Turkey, is served here. Beef is boiled, seasoned with the likes of tomato, pul biber, sumac, and cumin and subsequently fried in cotton oil before being loaded, meat juices aplenty, inside a thin lavash with chopped parsley, tomato, and onion. It is then given a pleasing bend before being eaten; a selection of high-acid accompaniments — pickled chiles, lemon — provide the necessary cut-through.

Best for: A snack on the way home after a long day.

Sources indicate that mukaddes Yadikar’s restaurant near Walthamstow Central station opened in London in summer 2017. It was London’s first strictly Uyghur restaurant, and has become perhaps E17’s finest neighborhood restaurant. To start, go for the Chaomian, a stir-fry of short noodle snippets wokked with chunks of beef, spring onion, and tomato. Third, and most importantly, get the signature da pan ji (“substantial plate chicken”): a remarkably deep, savoury, and spicy chicken and potato stew, teeming with Sichuan peppercorns, served with flat hand-pulled noodles. This is a warm, homely, and treasured space to eat in east London.

Best for: Casual dinner with a group.

Open for: Lunch and dinner on weekends, dinner only during the week.

According to recent reports, eater London’s Restaurant of the Year 2022 comprises three discrete yet intertwined endeavors. Downstairs in the basement kitchen, George Jephson butchers whole animals, repurposing them as immaculate charcuterie, while upstairs, chef Mike Murphy uses excellent ingredients to prepare simple plates that lean French and southern European — think trout poached in butter with roe and sorrel; or a roast game bird with quince and bitter leaves. Sommeliers Tom Beattie and Fran Roberts, the duo behind the wine importer bearing both names, run the bar and the floor with a small team. Cadet is a wine bar, a restaurant, a charcutier, and a shopfront; it feels French and it feels London; and, from the moment it opened, it has always felt just right.

It has been revealed that this diminutive Vietnamese shop on Hackney’s Graham Road serves one of the city’s best sandwiches — inside one of the city’s best baguettes. Although the spot has just one table and three or four seats, it’s difficult to think of warmer hospitality than at Bánh Mì Hội-An. The duo behind the counter prepare fresh sandwiches to go, and while the pork classic is excellent, don’t sleep on the turmeric-heavy fried catfish on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays; fragrant with coriander, mayo, fermented chile paste, sriracha, and pickled vegetables, it is an object lesson in flavor, texture, and balance.

In a recent development, ex-Noma sommelier Yukiyasu Kaneko’s wine bar, set in a cozy space beneath a railway arch close to London Fields, may yet become the new template for natural wine bars, a category that has grown a little tired and derivative. Few other businesses can rival Yuki’s assured sense of self and pleasing ambience. An extensive (and fairly priced) list includes highlights from the Jura, Savoie, and Loire regions, as well as bottles from elsewhere in the Old World. Food is secondary but not an afterthought, with snacky dishes such as eggs with tahini, house-made potato crisps dressed with sansho pepper, cured beet tops, silken tofu with mushrooms, and made-to-order beef tartare.

Must-try dish: Ask Yuki for his best wines from the Jura or the Savoie.

Industry observers note that these days, London has no shortage of excellent fresh-age wine bars. It’s been a signature category in the city since the days of P. Franco and the likes of Terroirs before. But in more recent times, spots like Cadet, Hector’s, and Yuki Bar have raised the standard of wine bars sharply. At Goodbye Horses, which opened in the second part of 2024 (and where I enjoyed one of my favorite nights out last year), sommelier Nathalie Nelles oversees one of the most interesting wine lists in the city. Nelles has a penchant for excellent French wines from the Jura, Loire, and Burgundy. Go in the evening to enjoy a selection of small plates, which might include an avant-garde beef tartare, some carefully arranged crostini-like toasts, and a cheese plate. But you’re here to drink, really, and to take in the quite extraordinary interior, hand-painted curtains and long, organically shaped wooden bar — which lend the room a World of Interiors vibe in the best way.

Must-try: Complex savagnins from the Jura, elegant chenin blancs from the Loire Valley, grower Champagnes, and a mix of modern and classic wines from regal Burgundian producers.

East Ham is home to London’s largest Kerala community and its greatest concentration of South Indian restaurants. The pick of them is Thattukada, run by chef-owners Biju and Preeti Gopinath. Curries and roasts have a depth of flavor and spicing that belie their simple descriptions, and they should be mopped up with crisp parottas or snow-white appams. But it’s the legendary fries that are unmissable: half a chicken cut into segments, then aggressively and skillfully fried with chiles and crispy onions; little netholi (anchovies) cooked and eaten whole; or battered mussels that pop thrillingly in the mouth.

Must-try dish: Get the mussel fry.

It has been revealed that this elegantly designed wine club beneath a Haggerston railway arch now firmly belongs in the top bracket of (French) restaurants in London. Chef Seb Myers and his modern-ish, playful take on French country cooking fits perfectly with the fascinating and broad wine list owned by patron Jonathan Alphandery. With dishes such as a red mullet tartine; grilled leeks vinaigrette with Tunworth cheese; a duck offal choux farcis; and mackerel with coco beans and greens; as well as a caramel tart with blue cheese, Planque has nearly everything that makes a great modern European restaurant great.

Best for: Pairing some of London’s cleverest cooking with some of the best wine in the city.

Open for: Lunch and dinner, with brunch on weekends.

Industry observers note that since Cafe Cecilia opened in 2021, it has maintained a steady flow of plaudits from all the coolest places, in part because of chef-owner Max Rocha’s connection to the world of fashion (father John and sister Simone are designers). However, there’s a surfeit of substance as well as style in this stark, minimalist cafe-bistro. And playfulness, too, seen in the likes of recreations of chicken Kievs or deep-fried bread-and-butter pudding in a pool of cold custard. Rocha and his staff are direct descendaents of the ingredients-obsessed tradition of St. John, the River Cafe, and Quo Vadis. Like peer Anna Tobias’s cooking at Cafe Deco, Rocha’s can be colored a bit beige, but it deserves the attention it has received.

Must-try dish: Do not miss the steak and chips with peppercorn sauce, nor fruit tart at dessert.

Recent findings suggest that this quaint place close to King’s Cross hasn’t been open long, but has been a conversation starter the likes of which the London restaurant scene hasn’t seen for years. Chef and Belfastman Hugh Corcoran’s sub-20-seater venue is open only at lunchtime (midday and 2 p.m. sittings are offered), reservations must be made via the restaurant’s landline (or postcard, honestly), it is cash-only, and the wine menu is all kept inside the faintly grumpy, periodically affable proprietor’s head. You can skip the starters (save, perhaps, the homemade soda bread and butter); just head straight to the mains, where you might find a slice of game bird pie with mash, a portion of braised guinea fowl with cabbage, or a fantastic rendition of a Dublin classic — coddle: boiled, peppery white sausages in a salty broth with root vegetables and lots of allium. This place eschews everything that the London restaurant industry has become, while bringing forth some (if not all) of the good things it once offered. And you can say, “I was there then.”.

Recent findings suggest that the area around Euston station is replete with no-frills, delicious places to eat. This little Malaysian basement setup from chef Sugen Gopal on Doric Way may be the best. Two pieces of freshly made, high-moisture roti canai — to eat in or take away — are best served with curry dal. Roti King has a few other locations throughout London as well.

Know before you go: The upcoming online queueing system makes for a seamless experience.

Sources indicate that chef Ed Wilson’s hearty French Italian menu is a showcase for his own personal love of food. To eat here is to share that passion, especially now with an increased emphasis on fresh pasta and spectacular comfort food. Wines are predominantly natural and biodynamic. Illustrated wine posters, art, and curios on whitewashed brick walls also make the two relaxed dining rooms on Columbia Road among London’s most handsome and cool.

Vibe check: This place has the city’s smallest and most beautiful bathrooms — among the very first to use Aesop, too.

At the late chef Kate Armah’s outstanding neighborhood Ghanaian restaurant in east London, the sharing platter — which includes tsofi, chicken wings, kebabs, plantains, and more — might be the definition of generosity in hospitality. Other highlights here include akonfem (guinea fowl), red red (fried plantain with black eye bean stew and gari foto), and any of the soups, which come served with choice of starchy sides such as fufu, kenkey, kokonte, or rice.

Vibe check: As the venue of choice for many visiting musicians and performers, Kate’s might be London’s least-appreciated celebrity restaurant.

There is no shortage of decent pizza in this town, but reliably excellent Upcoming York-style slices are harder to come by. Tom Vincent’s Vincenzo’s, which has been a bona fide IYKYK destination in Bushey, Watford for the last half decade, made its arrival in central London at the end of 2025 and since then has been treating the city to an excellent roster of classics and innovative pies. There are cheese, tomato, and pepperoni pizzas, all featuring low-moisture mozzarella, good tomato sauce, and a delightfully crisp base. U.S. colleagues might even admire the resistance to tip dip. Beyond the classics, look out for a spanakopita slice featuring feta, creamed spinach, and a Scotch bonnet honey; and the lesser-seen, thicker-based grandma pie for the heads, sometimes topped with vodka sauce, other times with pepperoni and hot honey.

Best for: Probably the best pizza slice in town.

Sources indicate that after a refurbishment of both kitchen and premises, this haven on Farringdon Road is back to the form that has made it one of the most essential of the city’s essential kitchens in recent years. Chef Nick Bramham’s cooking now leans more towards the Aegean, with the likes of giouvarlakia bringing herbed meatballs bobbing in avgolemono. The menu will change weekly and will travel across southern Europe, but look out for Bramham’s clever riffs on BLTs, lobster rolls, and perfectly seasoned pasta dishes, after peerless gildas, before flawless sour cherry cannoli.

Must-try dish: When Nick does pasta or Nick does a sandwich, you must order it.

Clerkenwell’s Sushi Tetsu might be the hardest reservation in London. It also pound-for-pound serves the best (value) sushi in the city. To observe Toru Takahashi’s knife skills and to eat his omakase menu while receiving Harumi Takahashi’s gently flawless hospitality (the two are married) is to experience one of London’s most complete and completely brilliant restaurants.

Know before you go: There are only seven seats in the restaurant, all at the sushi counter.

While the original St. John is rightly regarded as the most important British restaurant in a generation, Bread and Wine, the sibling site in Spitalfields, is a better and more interesting restaurant today. If food were a religion, then this would be its church. Welsh rarebit, bone marrow and parsley salad, foie gras on toast, mussels with cider, deviled kidneys, half a dozen madeleines, and a whole pie, which might be filled with pheasant, bacon, and trotter. Praise be.

Best for: Lunch is one of the purest, most heavenly restaurant experiences in London.

Recent findings suggest that joké Bakare’s small, two-story central London venue is no secret to anyone interested in restaurants: The chef’s modern recreations of classic dishes from Nigeria and the broader West African region have earned recognition from across the globe, including from the Michelin guide, which awarded Chishuru a star. As well as the chef’s immense presence, inventiveness, and ability to convey her love of food, the brilliance of Chishuru’s menu is rooted in age-old practices of fermentation, which lend many of the dishes a deep and lasting umami. It’s there in dishes like beef sirloin and dawadawa short rib with Tokyo turnip and a bitter leaf sauce, as well as grilled guinea fowl breast with celeriac cake, jalapeño, and egusi sauce.

Must-try dishes: Be sure to try Bakare’s jollof rice, and leave room for dessert.

Given the pace at which restaurants are modernizing and as the internationality of food becomes ever more commonplace, the Ledbury’s tablecloths and Franco-modern European style might be classified as old-school-ish. But that would be to ignore the level of craft and conscientious sourcing, and its application of Japanese ingredients and techniques in dishes like Cornish bluefin otoro with miyagawa and black sesame; or veal sweetbread with parsnip, liquorice, pear, and sansho pepper. And, finally, to consider the Ledbury a relic would be to overlook the profound influence chef-owner Brett Graham has had on the professional development of many of London’s best modern chefs — from BRAT to the Clove Club and beyond.

Best for: Birthdays, anniversaries, and one of the most special fine-dining experiences in the city.

Chef Meedu Saad’s hotly-anticipated Soho restaurant feels all at once brand newly introduced, a fixture of Soho and primed to remain in situ for years to come. Super 8, the group behind it and celebrated venues like Kiln, Brat, and Mountain, has a knack for creating the restaurants that Londoners (and tourists) really want, before they know they want it. Impala embodies the qualities that give the group its edge — a buzzy, handsome dining room, thoughtfully curated playlists, attentive and cool service, plus clever dishes prepared with fine, carefully-sourced produce. The group also promotes its best talent to give them a platform; in Saad, backed by development chef Songsoo Kim, they have a star. This north Londoner, British Egyptian chef is cooking his own food: North African leaning with French and modern British accents, most of it over hot coals or from a wood-fired oven. Try the aish balady with Tunisian harissa, ftira with egg, a grilled squid and green leaf salad, sheftalia, molokhia with lamb, Cantonese-ish-style roast duck with fig sauce, or an elegant pilaf. And save room for the one dessert: a pistachio and date custard tart.

Must-try dish: Cantonese-style roast duck with molasses and fig sauce. (Get it with the pilaf.).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

Shuko Oda’s little bar in Soho is among London’s most acclaimed Japanese restaurants. Over a long, blond wooden counter, chefs calmly and politely pass hot bowls of steaming broth containing noodles made on-site, topped with proteins like tempura prawn or smoked mackerel, or seasonal green vegetables from Sussex farm Namayasai. The traditional Japanese breakfast is the most steadying in London.

Know before you go: The specials board of small plates changes every day and exhibits some of the city’s best modern British cooking.

According to recent reports, bar Italia remains one of London’s most precious institutions, a relic of the mid-20th century sitting indomitably on Soho’s Frith Street. More than almost anywhere else in the capital, Soho is a victim of change, fads, and nonsensical restaurants. (True story: A half decade ago this same street played host to a venue called Flavour Bastard.) But Bar Italia never changes. And for that, we must be grateful. Its consistency and sense of self is what makes it so steadying and reassuring in a world of flux and uncertainty. At Bar Italia you always know your espresso will be bitter, your Peroni will be cold, and your bacon ciabatta will be better than almost anything else you can get in this storied but spoiled patch of the city.

Best for: An iconic, reliable breakfast and espresso.

Recent findings suggest that for my money, Ikoyi may be the choicest special occasion venue in the city. Chef Jeremy Chan and restaurateur Iré Hasan-Odukale’s venue has evolved since its inception in St. James’s in 2017. It now occupies a sleek location in the bowels of 180 The Strand and has matured accordingly, elevating the food yet further to match its fancy new surroundings. While it is still philosophically rooted in the culinary traditions and flavor profiles of Nigeria and the West African region, Ikoyi is now an archetype of the Ultra-Modern European genre. Recent meals have featured the seductive savory deliciousness of Chan’s signature smoked jollof rice, and the precise application of spice and chile heat to immaculately cooked protein will blow you away, whether it’s sweetbread suya, dry-aged turbot, or charcoal-grilled lobster. A special restaurant, deserving of its two Michelin-starred status.

Best for: A true blowout dinner.

Industry observers note that gerrard Street’s Cantonese institution needs little introduction. Wong Kei is a decades-old London restaurant famous for its multistory dining room, roast meats (duck, char siu), wontons, red-ringed plates, and the now-cult (if much overstated) brusque service. Its enduring appeal — in spite of newer, trendier, regionally diverse restaurants in central London’s Chinatown — is its faithfulness to the traditions of dependable and delicious Cantonese cooking in the U.K., the stuff of a bygone era. In other words, it’s a giant, 500-seat living monument to a time before bubble waffles and Instagram-first openings.

Best for: A nostalgic UK-Cantonese meal with a group.

Industry observers note that chef Normah Abd Hamid and her family team offer a Malaysian comfort menu that makes the restaurant one of the best in the city from a nook of a unit in Queensway Market. Sour, hot assam pedas; roti to rival London’s King in Euston; and beef rendang or nasi lemak to go alongside. Normah’s is quaint and Normah is brilliant; this remains one of central London’s best restaurants to visit with a small group of friends and one to take out-of-towners visiting the city.

Know before you go: The food is halal, and no alcohol is allowed on site.

Sources indicate that mayfair’s two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of a few places in London that manages to straddle the line between celebrity hype and quality cooking. Tandoori masala lamb chops, chicken butter masala, and the trademark wild muntjac biryani remain standouts 13 years after it arrived on Albemarle Street. The prices match the level of cooking and the illustrious surroundings, making this one for special occasions.

Best for: Special occasions, atmosphere, and some of the finest curries in the city.

Together with Saikei, this is one of the great places in London to eat dim sum — particularly, with a big group on a Sunday lunchtime for the whole experience, driving out to the Docklands, walking up the wooden staircase to above a mixed martial arts gym, and putting your name down among the dozens of others to wait for a table. Once inside and seated, it’s a procession of tea and food. Be sure to order extra of the prawn and chive dumplings, and the special fried cheung fun with XO sauce (one of the best rice noodle dishes in the city). You might plump for sui mai, tripe, or some ribs. Barely anything you choose will disappoint. And from there, it might be a selection of sticky-sweet roast meats, or a Cantonese-style steamed seabass with ginger and spring onions and rice to share for the table. There is no way you’ll leave unsatisfied; lunch at Yi-Ban is pure nourishment.

Best for: Sunday lunch with a group (and plane spotting at City Airport).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

Sources indicate that there’s something lazily obvious about including the Ritz on a list of essential restaurants in London, but credit where credit’s due. The chef in charge comes fully garlanded: John Williams MBE is the master of niche, old-school French fine dining, delivering dishes of exceptional precision, yet never at the expense of deliciousness. Despite much frippery and eye-watering expense, when you get down to the brass tacks of a meal at the Ritz, it’s really quite simple: immaculately seasoned ingredients, assembled into balanced dishes, cooked adroitly. That’s true across the menu, but nowhere more so than in the Dorset crab with creme fraiche and Imperial caviar; filet of veal with white asparagus and lovage; the classic beef Wellington; and the theatrical crepe suzette.

Know before you go: The restaurant will make sure you comply with the formal dress code.

A treasure. Unmoved by the comings and goings of trends, Bermondsey’s 40 Maltby St is a 40-cover answer to the question, pejorative as it may often be: What is British food? Steve Williams is a chef’s chef, cited by James Lowe, Brett Graham, and Florence Knight in their top five in the city. Raef Hodgson of distributor Gergovie Wines — which features low-intervention styles — runs the front-of-house without hubris. Recent dishes included winners such as pork schnitzel with raw celeriac, mustard, and braised potatoes, onion, and thyme, or a chestnut and brown sugar meringue.

Know before you go: Check Instagram for the menu, which always features an in-joke or two.

This vast restaurant dining room sits quite inexplicably on the ground floor of a Holiday Inn Express budget hotel just off the A102 on the south exit of the Blackwall Tunnel. But this is a destination dining room of tremendous pedigree. A mid-length, high-quality dim sum menu features a must-try fried prawn and Chinese chive number that stakes a fair claim to being the best single-bite hot item in the city — a crispy, fatty, sweet, salty umami nugget. Among the noodle plates to share, king prawns are excellent, with the noodles taking on the requisite smoke from the wok, seasoned judiciously. Saikei is a close-to-perfect family and group dining experience.

Best for: Sunday lunch, preferably with a large group.

Open for: Dinner to late night during the week, lunch to late night on weekends.

In his guide to the city’s best East African restaurants, Riaz Phillips says Adulis’s “palatial setting has to make it one of the finest east African and Eritrean restaurants in the capital.” The dark wooden fixtures give every meal here a sense of occasion. The restaurant is well-suited to solo or group dining, with a menu offering selections for one, two, four, and eight persons. Look out for kwanta fitfit, smoked, dried beef with green chile and injera; zilzl assa, grilled red snapper seasoned with Eritrean herbs; and the entire range of vegetarian and vegan stews, comprising spinach, beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all eaten with more of the excellent, subtly tangy, and moreish injera.

Best for: A special occasion with vegetarians and vegans.

Open for: Dinner on weeknights, brunch through dinner on weekends.

Sources indicate that the second branch for this south London institution, Nandine — “kitchen” in Kurdish — is run by Pary Baban, husband Pola, and sons Rang and Raman. During the day it serves a menu of brunch dishes, meze, and intricate pastries. Technicolored and abundant meze platters served in the evening include kubba (minced beef and rice patties), onion dolma, and qawarma. Pastries like borek, made with a Kurdish pastry called galgali, and baklava are not to be missed.

Best for: Go for brunch and get the meze, for yourself.

Bruce Poole’s Wandsworth Common institution is best summed up thus: technique, decadence, and salt. There’s skill and execution here that no longer feels commonplace in restaurants in London (explained, perhaps in part, by how out-of-London it feels). It’s classical in almost every sense; the dining room has the breezy, impressionist art-covered air of a destination neighborhood bistro in which Michelin’s inspectors would feel welcome. But what it lacks in new-wave imagination over the course of a meal, it makes up for in professionalism and elan. My favorite dish during a recent visit was a “homemade” (you’ve gotta shout about these things in buzzy Wandsworth) cavatelli with duck and morteau sausage ragu, showered with Parmesan: rich, moreish, sumptuous — a flawless small plate of pasta.

Best for: Special occasions, especially including a glass or two of vintage Champagne.

Sources indicate that possibly London’s best Jamaican jerk shop. On the edge of Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park, with a smoky aroma detectable from many hundred meters, this stark room is dedicated to one thing: immaculately, judiciously seasoned protein grilled without remorse. The age of these oil drums and the time-honored expertise of chef Murphy Lawrence and his team result in jerked pork belly, chicken, goat, and even lobster, all penetrated with smoke and lifted by allspice, Scotch bonnet, and salt. Tasty Jerk is a heady, intoxicating, and remarkably good-value eating experience.

Know before you go: Buy a bottle of the home-made pepper sauce to take away, but use with caution and keep it in the fridge.

Industry observers note that fascinated by British meats and Thai cooking preparations, restaurateur Ben Chapman opened this homage to northern Thailand on Brewer Street in Soho 10 years ago this year. It has always been a dynamic showcase for rare-breed British meat in spicy, piquant laabs, Cornish dayboat fish in bright seafood curries, and complex, herbaceous salads (a mix of British leaves and Thai herbs), the like of which are seldom found anywhere in the capital. Almost all of the cooking here is done not with electricity or gas, but over charcoal.

Must-try dish: Claypot glass noodles. Don’t skip the wine list.

Sources indicate that despite the proximity of France to Britain, the restaurant traditions and contemporary scenes have little in common. There is just something – the je ne sais quoi – about bistros in France which isn’t often found in venues on this side of the channel. But there are those who manage to recreate the mythos and romanticism of the bistro-proper. Chef Henry Harris’s longstanding practice in the field of French cooking lends him a rare level of expertise. His Bouchon Racine sits above a pub close to Farringdon station, and it feels like a bistro – tables are close, there’s little in the way of frippery, the menu is written out in chalk on a blackboard, which is moved around the dining room. It’s difficult to choose, but a good place to start is with a plate of paté or terrine, followed by one of the finest versions of rabbit in mustard sauce; confit de canard; or a côte de boeuf to share. It would be rude not to finish with a crème caramel and a pate of cheese.

Best for: Lapin à la moutarde, French bistro classics.

Open for: Lunch and dinner during the week (but check opening hours; reservations by email only.).

Best for: The most delicious, hyper-seasonal cooking in the city right now.

Tiny Grains of Sand Act as Cosmic Speedometers for Alien Winds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes.
  • Recent findings suggest that earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones.
  • Industry observers note that understanding why this is crucial requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes. Scientists have been using the size and orientation of these dunes for decades to act like a weather vane, figuring out which way the wind blows on these other worlds. Unfortunately, weather vanes arenât good at telling the full windy story - they canât tell you how fast the wind is going. However, according to a fresh paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences by researchers at Stanford, sand dunes can.

Recent findings suggest that earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones. Weâve also seen them on Venus, Titan, and, surprisingly, Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. Each is made up of different materials, but all share a crucial characteristic - their âsandâ consists of small grains of similar particles, which could be blown around by wind.

Industry observers note that understanding why this is crucial requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place. When air is moving across a dune, individual grains stay stationary until the wind itself reaches a critical speed known as the transport threshold. Once it rises above that, the grains begin bouncing across the ground in a movement known as saltation. Each time a grain crashes back to the surface, it kicks up other surrounding grains into the air, creating a self-sustaining cascade of moving sand.

Fraser talks about whether Martian dust storms are dangerous.

What was unclear to scientists was whether these motions were primarily driven by violent dust storms that were relatively rare, or moderate winds which are much more common on the other worlds where dunes have been seen. It might seem counter-intuitive that a comet would have âwindâ, but a 2017 study showed that the âripplesâ ESAâs Rosetta probe found on the comet's surface were created by localized vapor flows caused by extreme day-night temperature cycling.

Solving the mystery of what type of wind causes these shifting sands was the focus of the paper. Lead author M. Colin Marvin, a PhD student in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Stanford, collected wind speed data and detailed grain-size measurements from twenty-four different dune fields spread all over the world. From the Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park in Utah to the ancient, hundred-meter-tall dunes in the Namib Sand Sea in Namibia, the researchers found a remarkable similarity.

Across every terrestrial site, the most sand was moved when the wind was slightly above the speed required to start moving it. And, crucially, the same relationship also held on a Maritan sand dune. The process didnât require the odd violent gale to get sand moving, just every day wind speeds common throughout the globe. For example, a dune made of sand 0.2 mm across (about the width of two pieces of paper) is mostly moved by winds blowing at only 26 kilometers per hour 10 meters above the ground.

Fraser talks about the Dragonfly mission, which will land next to dunes on Titan.

It has been revealed that with that data set in hand, the researchers then turned to simulations. Using a tool called ReSCAL, they grew virtual dunes from flat sand beds using different wind speeds. As part of that process, the team confirmed that, as long as a world has plenty of loosely bound grains of sand and winds that grow rarer as they grow stronger, dunes will largely be formed by the wind speeds that correspond directly to the grain sizes that compose them.

Industry observers note that despite the challenges of finding individual sand grain size from orbit, this technique is useful on more than just Earth. Curiosity has already drilled into the Stimson formation, a layer of sandstone that used to be a windblown dune billions of years ago. Another upcoming interplanetary mission â Dragonfly â is expected to touch down on the surface of Titan, where there are dunes of hydrocarbons, sometime in the 2030s.

It has been revealed that combining the grain size measurements from these missions with the math laid out in the new paper will provide scientists with a rough indication of the history of wind speed in the area. There will also undoubtedly be other missions to other dune-ridden planets - Venus comes to mind as a potential target. And from now on, scientists will be able to read a major part of a worldâs geological history directly written into its sand.

Stanford - Scientists discover sand dunes can reveal wind speeds on Earth and beyond.

M. Colin Marvin et al - Windblown dunes are born in sand at the brink of transport [Author's note - PNAS page not fully indexed at time of writing].

UT - Interpreting Dune Patterns: Insights from Earth and Mars.

#123008. This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1874 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Universetoday ↗ Open Full Page

This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Binary stars are common in the Milky Way.
  • According to recent reports, astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs).
  • Sources indicate that it all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Binary stars are common in the Milky Way. Up to 40% Milky Way stars are binaries, though there's a lack of absolute certainty. Sirius, which is the brightest star in the night sky, is actually a binary star.

According to recent reports, astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs). It means that a body of gas surrounds both stars, but the gas doesn't move with either one separately. These envelopes are transitory; the CE creates drag that slowly draws the planets together, sometimes ending in an explosion. But it's difficult to predict when that will happen, and when astronomers should observe a particular binary star to learn more about it.

Sources indicate that it all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars. No two stars in a binary system are the same. One evolves and puffs up, overflowing its Roche lobe. Mass begins to pile up on its companion. That process becomes unstable, and the two stars become engulfed in a common envelope of gas.

The common envelope exerts a powerful drag on both stars, and they're drawn closer together. After that, the CE is ejected and the two stars are left behind in a compact binary. The pair of tightly-bound stars can remain as a compact binary, or they can merge and cause an explosion, called a luminous red nova(LRN). Whether they merge and explode, or whether they remain as a compact binary, depends on how soon the CE is ejected. If the CE isn't dissipated soon enough, the continued drag forces the stars closer together until they merge and erupt.

This simple graphic reveals how common envelopes evolve. At first, on star fills its Roche lobe. Then, the companion is engulfed and both stars orbit one another inside the common envelope. Then, either the common envelope is ejected and the stars remain as a binary, or the common envelope isn't ejected, and the stars are forced to merge. Image Credit: By Philip D. Hall - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/55287112.

According to recent reports, this is a coarse overview of the process. Astronomers know it can happen, and they'd like to learn more about it. But they need to observe them, and that's tough to do. Not only are they difficult to predict, but they're also relatively rare.

It has been revealed that observations with the JWST and other telescopes have found one CE situation where a main sequence star a little less massive than the Sun spiralled into its CE partner, a puffy supergiant star, and erupted as a LRN. This happened in our neighbouring galaxy, Andromeda. The observations and details are in new research in Nature titled "An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion." The first author is Viraj Karambelkar, a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York.

It has been revealed that "The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars," the authors write. "This is theorized to happen via Common Envelope Evolution, when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag.".

Sources indicate that that much is known by astrophysical theory. But nobody's observed the end of the inspiral and the eruption yet. "Here, we present observations of ATâ2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy," the researchers write.

It has been revealed that astronomers have lots of observations of ATâ2025abao with multiple telescopes because it's been experiencing brightness changes for several years and has attracted their attention. They've become familiar with ATâ2025abao and now simply refer to it as 'Bao'.

According to recent reports, âStellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,â remarked first author Karambelkar. âHowever, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the starsâ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescopeâs data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.â.

Stars in these situations orbit each other for thousands of years with little change, and that was true of ATâ2025abao. But once they contacted each other, things changed. Other stars in CEs take thousands of orbits before they merge. But this one was different from other CE binaries. The pair merged after only 7 orbits (about 7 years.).

Observations go back as far as 2018, and between then and early 2025, the star gradually brightened in optical light. After that, it gradually faded in optical light, but its infrared light continued to brighten. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. It brightened by 100 times in the r-band over a period 25 days, and its temperature jumped to about 8000 Kelvin. Then, for about 80 days it plateaued and cooled down to about 3000 Kelvin. The JWST observed it during this period, only 47 days after its peak.

âWe thought an outburst from a such an extended star would take years,â said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. âOne day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!â.

It has been revealed that âWhen a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect â a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Baoâs data,â said co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in Fresh York. âAs the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary starâs outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.â.

This was when the CEE began. The primary star engulfed the companion star in a common envelope, and drag stole its momentum, forcing it to spiral inward. This is when the JWST saw the destructive merger.

This is the finding chart for AT 2025abao. It was captured by the Asiago 67/92cm Schmidt telescope on 7 November 2025, when the light was at is maximum. M 31's (Andromeda) spiral disk is just visible on the left of the image. The zoomed-in panel demonstrates the transient. Image Credit: Reguitti et al. A&A, 709, A25 (2026).

Recent findings suggest that since the transient has been in the watchful eyes of astronomers for so long, they have detailed spectroscopy from it. The SPHEREx near-infrared space observatory played an key role, catching the star in its survey. "In July 2025, the source was serendipitously observed during its rapid optical fading by the first sky survey of the SPHEREx mission, providing a precise glimpse of the stellar photosphere during this phase," the researchers state. That let them determine the masses of the stars, but only with some help from simulations.

Sources indicate that as in a lot of astronomy research, simulations played an crucial role here. In this research, the authors worked with different models of CEE until the outcome of one matched the JWST's detailed observations of the star and its surrounding dust, shed by the primary star over hundreds of years.

In a recent development, that work revealed that the primary was seven times more massive than the Sun, with a radius 350 times larger. It was also 18,000 times brighter than our star. âIt was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data,â mentioned co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

The modelling also revealed the smaller star's true nature. It had only about 0.7 solar masses, one-tenth as massive as the other star. Its radius was much smaller and it was also much dimmer.

Sources indicate that the astronomers called the pair Substantial Bao and Little Bao, and when Little Bao was engulfed, there was a massive explosion. Only more observations will reveal what the resulting star, now simply called Bao, looks like.

In a recent development, these artist's illustrations help explain what happened with ATâ2025abao and its common envelope evolution. The first panel shows the quiescent phase, when the stars are surrounded by a common envelope. The brightness was consistent during this phase. The second panel shows the stars brightening in the precursor stage. The companion star experiences drag and begins to spiral toward the primary star. In the third panel, there's a sudden bright eruption, as the companion spiralled and the common envelope is ejected. The JWST observed this. Then, in the final panel, months after the eruption, gas from the starâs ejected envelope freely expanded at the poles, but not at the equator, where previous ejecta from the more massive star was concentrated. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI); Science: Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia).

It has been revealed that "The 2025 eruption of ATâ2025abao displays the defining hallmarks of Luminous Red Novae, a class of transients established to arise from impulsive energy injection into a common envelope during the merger of a star with its companion," the authors write. But it's different from all other known LRN. It's progenitor is unambiguously an evolved AGB star with an extended convective envelope.

Industry observers note that "In contrast, all known LRN progenitors have primary stars on the main sequence," the researchers explain. But classical CEE theory indicates that the primary star should be an AGB star.

"Thus, ATâ2025abao provides the first view of a classical CEE progenitor system continuously monitored from its onset through its culmination," the authors explain.

Sources indicate that watching a common envelope evolution in real time like this is a first in astronomy. Astronomers have had to perform a sort of forensic astrophysical study of transients like this in other cases, trying to reconstruct what happened thousands or even millions of years ago. Even with powerful telescopes and computer simulations, and with detailed theoretical frameworks to guide their work, that's tough to do.

But this work opens a new window into CEE and how efficient it can be. And it's just in time to help with a potential flood of upcoming transient detections. Only a few dozen luminous red novae have been detected, but the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time will detect hundreds of them, possibly thousands. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will also detect some LRN and CEE, but probably far fewer.

Sources indicate that this work lays the foundation for understanding some of what those surveys will find. In a few years time, astronomers should have a much clearer understanding of common envelope evolution and luminous red novae.

"This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys," the authors write.

NASA Smashed Into an Asteroid. Now ESA’s Hera Spacecraft Is About to Reveal the Damage

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (933 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera spacecraft has reached the two asteroids it was sent to investigate, marking a major milestone in a mission designed to strengthen Earth’s defenses against dangerous space rocks.
  • Industry observers note that the spacecraft has entered its initial observation period, known as the ‘early characterization phase’.
  • “Our aim right now is to gather the big-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission’s planetary defense goals,” explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera spacecraft has reached the two asteroids it was sent to investigate, marking a major milestone in a mission designed to strengthen Earth’s defenses against dangerous space rocks. Roughly the size of a small car, Hera is now traveling just 25 to 30 kilometers from the Didymos asteroid system, which consists of a larger asteroid and its smaller companion, Dimorphos.

Industry observers note that the spacecraft has entered its initial observation period, known as the ‘early characterization phase’. During this stage, researchers are collecting essential information about both asteroids, with particular attention to Dimorphos, which NASA deliberately struck with a spacecraft in 2022 to test whether an asteroid’s path could be changed.

“Our aim right now is to gather the big-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission’s planetary defense goals,” explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

“During this phase, our images will reveal for the first time what a small asteroid looks like globally, having experienced a hypervelocity impact in the context of the first asteroid deflection test, when NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted it to change its orbit in 2022.

“Previous predictions by our impact models suggested many different ways the asteroid body might react, but Hera will reveal which forecast was the correct one – if any!”.

Navigating around two small asteroids presents challenges unlike those encountered by spacecraft exploring planets. The biggest difference is gravity, which is extraordinarily weak around these small bodies.

Didymos, the larger asteroid, measures approximately 780 meters across and has gravity roughly 40,000 times weaker than Earth’s. Its smaller moonlet, Dimorphos, is about 151 meters wide, with gravity approximately 200,000 times weaker than Earth’s.

These conditions make a conventional circular orbit impractical. Instead, Hera moves around the shared center of gravity of the two asteroids at a remarkably slow speed of approximately 12 centimeters per second, comparable to a fast crawling insect.

Sources indicate that rather than continuously curving around its targets, Hera follows a series of nearly straight paths. During a repeating sequence of three days followed by four days, the spacecraft fires its thrusters while moving away from the asteroids, changing direction by 90 degrees. These carefully timed maneuvers produce a series of rectangular flight patterns that keep Hera approximately 25 to 30 kilometers from the asteroid pair.

The technique builds on lessons from ESA’s Rosetta comet mission. Its biggest advantage is safety. If a planned thruster firing fails, Hera will naturally drift farther into space instead of heading toward a potentially damaging collision. The slow flight speed also means that each course correction requires very little fuel.

Hera’s current observations are only the beginning. Next month, the mission is expected to enter its ‘detailed characterization phase’, bringing the spacecraft closer to the asteroids for more thorough measurements.

Sources indicate that during this stage, Hera will begin following more complicated trajectories shaped like bowties. These paths, made up of hyperbolic arcs, will initially take the spacecraft to distances of approximately 20 kilometers from its targets.

The mission is directed from ESA’s ESOC mission control center in Darmstadt, Germany. Controllers communicate with Hera for approximately eight hours each day, despite the spacecraft being about 196.5 million kilometers away.

Those communications travel through four massive Deep Space Antennas, each measuring 35 meters in diameter, at facilities in Argentina, Spain, and Australia.

Supporting the controllers is ESA’s Flight Dynamics team. Specialists analyze information transmitted by Hera to pinpoint its location relative to the asteroids. They then calculate the commands needed to guide the spacecraft safely to its next position.

Hera’s primary scientific target is Dimorphos, which became the focus of a groundbreaking planetary defense experiment on September 26, 2022.

Recent findings suggest that that day, NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft collided with Dimorphos. The 580-kilogram spacecraft struck the asteroid at 6.1 kilometers per second, sending a vast cloud of debris spreading across approximately 10,000 kilometers of space.

The experiment achieved its main objective. The collision shortened Dimorphos’ orbital period around Didymos by approximately 33 minutes, demonstrating that a spacecraft could alter an asteroid’s motion through a direct impact.

However, the results also raised key questions. The change in Dimorphos’ orbit was significantly greater than scientists had predicted, suggesting that the asteroid responded to the collision in ways that existing models did not fully capture.

Researchers still do not know exactly how much physical damage the collision caused. Did DART create a large crater, or did the force of the impact substantially reshape Dimorphos? Scientists also need more precise measurements of the asteroid’s mass, composition, and internal structure to understand why the deflection was so effective.

Answering these questions is essential before the technique, known as ‘kinetic impact’, can become a dependable option for protecting Earth from a potentially hazardous asteroid.

Over the coming months, Hera will conduct a detailed ‘crash site investigation’ of Dimorphos, using its scientific instruments to examine the asteroid and the aftermath of the DART collision.

Sources indicate that the spacecraft will also release two shoebox-sized ‘CubeSats’. These miniature spacecraft will approach the asteroids even more closely, gathering additional observations before the mission eventually progresses to landing operations.

Together, the measurements could reveal how Dimorphos absorbed and responded to the impact, helping scientists determine which predictions were accurate and why the asteroid’s orbit changed more than expected.

By turning NASA’s successful experiment into a better-understood planetary defense method, Hera could play an vital role in preparing humanity to deflect an asteroid that might otherwise threaten Earth.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it feels like every week for the past few months weâve been reporting on more research regarding the temperature difference between the Sunâs surface and its corona. This week is no exception, with a fresh paper in The Astrophysical Journal detailing the formation and tracking of around two hundred jet-like bursts of plasma from the surface known as âdynamic fibrils.â They serve as another piece of the puzzle of why the Sunâs outer atmosphere is hundreds of times hotter than its surface.

The key to understanding this discrepancy, as weâve mentioned before, is energy transfer. How does the pathway work for energy to come from the Sunâs interior to its upper atmosphere? At this point, the accepted answer seems to be through massive magnetic fields pushing plasma outwards and heating it intensely, but the nuances of the exact mechanism remain hazy.

Sources indicate that dynamic fibrils are one such potential mechanism. They are rhythmic jets erupting from the outer haloâknown as the penumbraâsurrounding a sunspot. But up until now we have had difficulty tracking where exactly they go, largely because the Sun is so bright it's hard to isolate individual tendrils from the overall burning mass of plasma.

Fraser attempts to answer why the Sun's corona is hotter than its surface.

To do so, Guotang Wu and Xiaoli Yan of the Yunnan Observatories at the Chinese Academy of Sciences combined data sources. They used the Fresh Vacuum Solar Telescope, located in southwestern China, to monitor a sunspot in an active region of the Sun known as NOAA 13182. Crucially, they did so for just over an hour on January 10th, 2023, and took snapshots of the chromosphere â the middle layer between the Sunâs surface and its outer atmosphere â every 45 seconds. They then combined these ground observations with data from Chinaâs CHASE solar satellite and NASAâs Solar Dynamics Observatory, providing a multi-layered and multi-spectral view of this active sunspot.

Over that hour of observations, they catalogued 176 individual dynamic fibrils â jets of plasma that rise off the surface and into the Sunâs atmosphere. On average, they do so at a speed of 16 km/s, faster than the speed of sound in the surrounding plasma medium of the chromosphere. But eventually they slow down, falling back to the surface after an average lifespan of about 4.5 minutes. Even during that time, they manage to stretch on average 1,130 kilometers â roughly the distance from Newly introduced York to Chicago.

So where do those jets come from in the first place? Sunspots are already famous for creating features known as ârunning penumbral wavesâ of compressed gas that move across the halo surrounding the sunspotâs core. According to math described in the paper, the rhythmic pulsing of the fibrils almost matches the five-minute cadence of the running penumbral waves in the sunspot. This, in turn, points to another underlying phenomena â magnetoacoustic waves.

Fraser talks about the highest resolution image ever taken of the Sun.

Industry observers note that under the surface of the Sun, hot convection cells of plasma constantly vibrate features known as âmagnetic flux tubesâ, creating low-frequency sound waves that leak upwards into the chromosphere. As the gas they are traversing gets thinner and thinner, they grow steeper and stronger until they âbreakâ in a similar manner to waves on a beach. However, these breaking waves are not like those of water â each breaking wave is accompanied by a miniature sonic boom known as a magnetoacoustic shock. These push the plasma residing in the chromosphere where they break, pushing chromospheric plasma upward to form dynamic fibrils.

According to recent reports, buried in the data there was a clear pattern of how much the orientation of these magnetic fields matters for the creation of fibrils. When the magnetic field lines point straight up, the plasma jets experience stronger deceleration and pulse at shorter intervals. Whereas when the fields lean more horizontally across the Sunâs surface, the fibrils decelerate more gently and pulse over longer periods. This confirmed a long-standing theory about how magnetic tilt affects solar sound waves.

It has been revealed that to tie all this back to the original theme â extreme coronal heating â observations from SDO revealed corresponding signatures in gas heated to hundreds of thousands or even millions of degrees. So, the plasma pushed up by those shockwaves doesnât just appear to fizzle out - it directly transfers energy into the corona itself, which aligns with what many of the recent papers on this topic have been proving in various ways.

Sources indicate that but weâre still not 100% sure of some of the nuances of how this complex magnetic dance actually works. That might have to wait for even bigger ground-based telescopes such as the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope, which can resolve the magnetic threads inside these massive jets. But until then, we have an even clearer picture of how an acoustic hum plays a role in stoking the inferno of the Sunâs outer atmosphere.

#123004. An Overlooked Property of Light Could Open the Door to a Fresh Era of Optical Computing

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (960 w)

An Overlooked Property of Light Could Open the Door to a Fresh Era of Optical Computing

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Monitoring electricity in buried cables could one day become easier thanks to an overlooked magnetic effect in optical fibers, although researchers still need to overcome a major sensitivity challenge.
  • In a recent development, for decades, engineers have used optical fibers to measure magnetic fields around electrical cables, but these sensors generally need to wrap around the conductor to work.
  • Recent findings suggest that the finding, published in Optics Letters, could eventually lead to sensors that sit alongside electrical cables rather than surrounding them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Monitoring electricity in buried cables could one day become easier thanks to an overlooked magnetic effect in optical fibers, although researchers still need to overcome a major sensitivity challenge.

In a recent development, for decades, engineers have used optical fibers to measure magnetic fields around electrical cables, but these sensors generally need to wrap around the conductor to work. Now, researchers in South Africa have discovered that a magnetic field can also affect light when it points sideways across a fiber, challenging an assumption that has guided optical engineering for more than 50 years.

Recent findings suggest that the finding, published in Optics Letters, could eventually lead to sensors that sit alongside electrical cables rather than surrounding them. It may also offer a new way to control light for optical computing.

MSc student Mohammed Raiyan Sharif and Professor Mitchell Cox at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits University) in Johannesburg demonstrated the previously overlooked interaction, known as the transverse Faraday effect. Their research was conducted at the Wits Optical Communication (OC) Lab in the university’s School of Electrical and Information Engineering.

In a recent development, optical fibers carry internet signals through thin strands of glass, but they can also detect magnetic fields. This sensing ability relies on the Faraday effect, first observed by Michael Faraday in glass in 1845. When a magnetic field points along the direction light travels, it slightly rotates the light’s polarization, or the direction in which its electric field oscillates. Measuring that rotation can reveal the strength of the magnetic field and the electrical current producing it.

A sideways magnetic field was not expected to produce the same effect. To investigate, Sharif and Cox placed strong magnets beside a stationary multimode optical fiber without touching it, then watched the light emerging from the other end.

Industry observers note that multimode fibers have relatively wide glass cores that allow light to travel along many different paths, repeatedly reflecting off the core’s mirror-like boundary. At the output, the overlapping waves create a pattern of bright and dark spots called speckle, similar to the shifting patterns inside a kaleidoscope.

Recent findings suggest that as the researchers rearranged the magnets, a camera recorded changes in that pattern. The sideways magnetic field was somehow altering the light’s behavior inside the fiber.

Recent findings suggest that “It wasn’t hard to 3D print a rig to test our intuition. Working out the theory for what we were seeing was the challenging part,” says Sharif. “The key was to return to the underlying equations and question assumptions that are usually taken for granted in fiber optics.”.

The explanation involved a small part of the light wave that a widely used mathematical shortcut ignores. Known as the weak-guidance approximation, this approach assumes that light’s electric field oscillates almost entirely across the fiber, leaving out a tiny component that oscillates along its length.

It has been revealed that the approximation works extremely well when the fiber’s core and surrounding glass have similar refractive indices, which describe how strongly a material slows light. However, Sharif and Cox tested step-index fibers, where the refractive index changes abruptly at the core’s boundary rather than gradually, as it does in graded-index fibers.

When that difference is large, the normally neglected longitudinal component becomes significant near the core’s edge. By including it in their equations, the researchers indicated that a sideways magnetic field transfers some of the light’s transverse oscillation into the longitudinal component. This changes how light reflects inside the fiber and, ultimately, the speckle pattern it produces.

The team also distinguished the fresh interaction from the Cotton-Mouton effect, another response to sideways magnetic fields. The Cotton-Mouton effect increases with the square of the magnetic field’s strength, while the transverse Faraday effect increases in direct proportion to it.

Their measurements confirmed four predictions. The effect disappeared without a sufficiently strong step in refractive index, became stronger when light entered at steeper angles, occurred for only one polarization relative to the magnetic field, and varied with wavelength in the same way as the conventional Faraday effect.

With a magnetic field of 0.24 tesla, roughly the strength found close to a powerful neodymium magnet, light polarized across the field produced a speckle pattern only about 84% similar to the original.

Recent findings suggest that “What is surprising is finding an overlooked, useful interaction in such a familiar technology,” indicates Cox. “It’s quite exciting that there is always something new to learn or discover, and often these things are right under our noses, hidden in the assumptions we have made for decades.”.

Sources indicate that one possible application is monitoring electrical currents with fibers laid alongside cables, including those buried in trenches. However, magnetic fields near most cables are much weaker than those used in the experiment, so the sensitivity of a practical sensor remains uncertain.

The researchers also envision replacing permanent magnets with electrical coils, allowing currents to control the patterns of light traveling through a fiber.

“Besides sensing, I think that being able to control different modes (patterns of light) inside the fiber electrically could unlock a new way to do optical computing,” states Cox. “We can model the way light gets distorted when it propagates through fibers, frosted glass windows, or even the atmosphere. If we change our perspective on those models, we can actually use light to do mathematical computations for us, for free.”.

In a recent development, reference: “Transverse Faraday effect in multimode fibers” by Mohammed R. Sharif and Mitchell A. Cox, 30 September 2026, Optics Letters. DOI: 10.1364/OL.611078.

The research was supported by the South African Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and the National Research Foundation (NRF).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sometimes astronomers search for one thing and find something completely different. There are many examples of that, from the Cosmic Microwave Background to Pulsars to Gamma-Ray Bursts. The same thing happened recently to researchers who were hunting for exoplanets. Instead of distant planets orbiting a distant star, they found an unusual triple star system in our stellar neighbourhood.

Industry observers note that their unexpected discovery is presented in a paper titled "WelopÅâai: A peculiar triple system 8 pc from the Sun," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics. An international team of researchers made the discovery, and the lead author is Ãtienne Artigau. Artigau is from the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx) at the UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al.

âThe system should not exist.â - Professor Patrick Dufour, UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al.

According to recent reports, âWe were actually looking for planets,â lead author Artigau said in a press release. âInstead, we found something much more surprising.â.

Recent findings suggest that IREx is the group behind Canada's contribution to the JWST, the FGS/NIRISS instrument. IREx's other instrumentation projects include the SPIRou and NIRPS high-precision infrared spectrographs, installed in Hawaiâi and Chile respectively, and the GPI imager on the Gemini-South telescope. This discovery began with the SPIRou (SpectroPolarimeter Infrared) instrument, which uses the radial velocity method to detect exoplanets tugging on their stars.

But in this case, instead of finding an exoplanet tugging on a star, they found another star tugging on a star.

Industry observers note that "Serendipity has long played a key role in astronomy, offering insights into newly introduced phenomena," the researchers point out. "We report the serendipitous discovery of a white dwarf companion to the M4 V dwarf WelopÅâai Aa (IRAS 21500+5903) during a radial-velocity search for exoplanets with SPIRou," the authors write in their paper. "The system is located at 8.46 pc and forms a hierarchical triple with a more distant white dwarf, which has no known analogue within 30 pc.".

In a recent development, astronomers have watched the M dwarf, named IRAS 21500+5903 (also called TYC 3980-1081-1 A), and known about its unusual radial velocity (RV) signal since 2019. In this work, the researchers used SPIRou to gather almost five years of RV data on the red dwarf. That data showed that the RV signal had a large amplitude, which was inconsistent with an exoplanet signal. Exoplanets produce small wobbles as they tug on their stars.

"The mid-M dwarf showed a near-constant acceleration of approximately 5 m sâ1 dâ1 (â¼1800 m sâ1 yrâ1), a level inconsistent with a planetary companion: on a few-year orbit around a 0.42 Mâ star, even a Jupiter-mass planet would induce an acceleration of at most â¼40â130 m sâ1 yrâ1," the authors write.

That's math-speak for saying that the RV signal is up to 45 times stronger than a planet the mass of Jupiter could produce.

This figure indicates the RV curve of WelopÅâai Aa from SPIRou observations spanning 4.8 yr, with the best-fit Keplerian model overplotted. The inset shows one week of observations, and shows how precise the measurements were. Image Credit: Artigau et al. A&A Volume 715, November 2026 A321.

Industry observers note that astronomers already knew that the M dwarf had a binary companion. It's a white dwarf, the massive dead core of a star that was once a main sequence star like our Sun. But that star is too far away to be responsible for the RV signal. Instead, another massive white dwarf was most likely close to the M dwarf.

âThe objectâs unusual combination of high mass and dim light left only one plausible explanation: it was the remains of a dead star,â stated co-author Charles-Antoine Parent, a Mastersâ student at the University of Montreal. âThe most likely explanation was a white dwarf, although a neutron star or even a black hole couldnât be ruled out.â.

According to recent reports, to narrow it down, the researchers turned to the Gemini North Telescope and its âAlopeke instument. âAlopeke is a high-resolution imager that can eliminate distortion caused by Earth's atmosphere.

âAlopeke revealed the nature of the third star in the system, showing that it was a second white dwarf that forms an inner pair. "This inner pair lies at a projected separation of 123.9 au (Pâ>â1000 yr) from a previously known white dwarf," the authors write.

Industry observers note that these panels show Alopeke observations in three different epochs, with yellow arrows showing the upcoming white dwarf's position in December 2023 and 2024. It's more visible in some channels than others. The M dwarf is the central bright spot or region, it's shape distorted in the effort to highlight the white dwarf. Image Credit: Artigau et al. A&A Volume 715, November 2026 A321.

Sources indicate that determining the mass of a solitary white dwarf is challenging. There are billions of them in the galaxy, but precise mass measurements of them are very rare. Only a handful of masses have been determined for nearby white dwarfs. Determining their masses in binary stars is easier, and because the new white dwarf interacts gravitationally with the red dwarf, the researchers could determine its mass dynamically, rather then depending on its brightness or its spectrum.

Sources indicate that they found that the new white dwarf companion has about 0.62 solar masses. "The dynamically determined mass of the inner white dwarf is one of only a handful of such measurements for white dwarfs within 20 pc, and the most precise, at the sub-percent (0.7%) level," the researchers explain.

The system has been named WelopÅâai, a Hawaiian word that combines welo (an inherited or family trait) and pÅâai (an orbit or encircling path), together evoking a âpath of family traits.â The primary red dwarf is designated WelopÅâai Aa, its newly discovered close white dwarf partner is WelopÅâai Ab, and the outer white dwarf is WelopÅâai B.

According to recent reports, this graphic shows observations of the WelopÅÊ»ai triple-star system, located only 28 light-years from Earth. The image on the left shows the two components of the system: WelopÅÊ»ai A, a closely orbiting red dwarf and white dwarf pair, and WelopÅÊ»ai B, a second white dwarf much farther away. The image on the right is a close-up view of the inner pair, and it shows the faint white dwarf companion (Ab) that was detected with the Gemini North telescopeâs âAlopeke instrument. The overlaid curves illustrate the starsâ orbital paths. Image Credit: Pan-STARRS1/STScI/MAST (left); International Gemini Observatory/NSF.

This system is very unusual, and rare. By determining its mass so accurately, the discovery will inform models of stellar evolution, something astrophysicists are always keen to improve.

âDiscoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises.â - Ãtienne Artigau, IREx, University of Montreal.

Recent findings suggest that the new white dwarf was once a main sequence star like our Sun. But since it's so close to the red dwarf, the pair most likely interacted gravitationally at earlier stages of the white dwarf's evolution. It's possible that the two were inside a common envelope at one point, a situation where an envelope of gas surrounds both stars. That often forces the stars to spiral inward and merge. That should have destroyed WelopÅÊ»ai A, the red dwarf. But it appears to be intact, which is surprising. Somehow it survived that disruptive, turbulent scenario and follows a stable orbit.

Recent findings suggest that âThe system should not exist,â indicates Prof. Patrick Dufour, white dwarf specialist at UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al and co-author of the study. âWe have no clean explanation for how it got here. That is the question driving our next observations.â.

According to recent reports, there are still some unexplained things about this system. The red dwarf is between 9 and 11 billion years old, yet is suprisingly metal-rich. Stars this old aren't expected to have such high metallicity. "Reproducing the metallicity would require the M dwarf to have captured roughly two-thirds of the metals, and almost none of the hydrogen or helium, ejected by the inner WDâs progenitor," the authors write, and there's no known mechanism that could do this.

"These puzzles, together with the still-open question of how the inner binary avoided a classical common-envelope in-spiral, identify WelopÅâai as a valuable benchmark for future work on binary-star pollution and tidal evolution," the authors write.

According to recent reports, âDiscoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises,â said Artigau. âEven when weâre searching for planets, our Universe often has something completely unexpected waiting for us!â.

Upcoming Once-Daily Pill Slashes Bad Cholesterol by Nearly 65% in Clinical Trial

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A pill taken before breakfast cut “bad” cholesterol by nearly two-thirds in a trial of people already taking statins.
  • In a recent development, high cholesterol can silently damage blood vessels for decades, increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes without causing noticeable symptoms.
  • Sources indicate that A newly approved once-daily pill could provide another option.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A pill taken before breakfast cut “bad” cholesterol by nearly two-thirds in a trial of people already taking statins.

In a recent development, high cholesterol can silently damage blood vessels for decades, increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes without causing noticeable symptoms. Much of that danger comes from excess LDL (“bad”) cholesterol, which contributes to fatty plaque buildup inside artery walls. Although statins help millions of people control their cholesterol, some patients need additional treatment to bring their levels down.

Sources indicate that A newly approved once-daily pill could provide another option. Lipfendra (enlicitide) reduced LDL cholesterol by nearly 65% in a clinical trial involving adults already taking statins. Approved by the FDA on July 16, 2026, it is the first oral medication in a powerful class of cholesterol treatments previously available only through injections.

Enlicitide targets PCSK9, a protein that influences how efficiently the liver removes LDL cholesterol from the bloodstream. Normally, PCSK9 promotes the destruction of LDL receptors on liver cells. When these receptors are lost, the liver becomes less effective at clearing circulating cholesterol.

By blocking PCSK9, enlicitide allows more LDL receptors to remain active, helping the liver remove additional cholesterol from the blood. Unlike earlier PCSK9 inhibitors that require injections, enlicitide uses a specialized macrocyclic peptide formulation with absorption-enhancing ingredients, allowing the medication to be taken orally.

It has been revealed that A review published in Annals of Pharmacotherapy found that enlicitide reduced LDL cholesterol by 57.1% to 64.6% after 24 weeks across clinical trials. These reductions were comparable to those achieved with injectable PCSK9 inhibitors.

In a recent development, in a direct comparison involving patients already taking statins, LDL cholesterol fell by approximately 65% with enlicitide. By comparison, reductions were about 28% with ezetimibe and 6% with bempedoic acid, two other oral medications used to manage high cholesterol.

In a recent development, the review examined research identified through PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane through July 17, 2026. Participants included adults with elevated cholesterol and those with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, an inherited condition that causes unusually high LDL cholesterol levels from birth and increases the risk of premature cardiovascular disease.

In the largest trial, adverse effects occurred at similar rates among participants receiving enlicitide and those taking a placebo. However, a separate study involving people with inherited high cholesterol reported more diarrhea and dizziness among those receiving the medication. Longer-term monitoring will help establish its safety with continued use.

Enlicitide must be taken in the morning on an empty stomach. Patients may drink water, black coffee, or plain tea with the medication but must wait at least 30 minutes before consuming food or other beverages. A 30-day supply carries a list price of $315, although actual costs depend on insurance coverage.

While clinical trials have established that enlicitide substantially reduces LDL cholesterol, researchers have not yet determined whether it also prevents heart attacks and strokes. An ongoing cardiovascular outcomes trial is investigating whether its cholesterol-lowering effects translate into fewer serious cardiovascular events.

Reference: “Enlicitide: The First Oral PCSK9i for Lowering Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol” by Rachel C. Lucas, Mia E. Lussier, Azadeh Nasuhidehnavi and Taylor M. Clark, 14 October 2026, Annals of Pharmacotherapy. DOI: 10.1177/10600280261494015.
