Latest Update: About three in four former NFL players who died from 2008 to 2023 had CTE

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh study estimates that about three in four former NFL players who died from 2008 through 2023 had CTE, even after accounting for brain donation bias.
  • Almost every former NFL player’s brain that researchers have examined has shown signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), the degenerative disease tied to repeated hits to the head.
  • The study estimated that families were more likely to donate a player’s brain if he had clear cognitive symptoms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh study estimates that about three in four former NFL players who died from 2008 through 2023 had CTE, even after accounting for brain donation bias.

Almost every former NFL player’s brain that researchers have examined has shown signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), the degenerative disease tied to repeated hits to the head.

The study estimated that families were more likely to donate a player’s brain if he had clear cognitive symptoms.

Researchers at Boston University have now worked out how much that choice skews the picture.

Industry observers note that the team’s estimate: about three in four NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had CTE. That includes the roughly five in six whose brains were not examined.

Industry observers note that three in four is lower than the figure from donated brains alone, where more than nine in ten had the disease. But the researchers noted the skew in who donates can’t explain the high rate away.

Julia Gallini, a doctoral candidate in biostatistics at the Boston University School of Public Health, led the analysis with Yorghos Tripodis, a professor of biostatistics there.

Colleagues at the university’s CTE Center, Mass General Brigham and the Concussion & CTE Foundation joined them.

The figure applies to players after death only and notes nothing about living former players or current ones.

Gallini said a precise number helps size the problem.

“An estimated 75% prevalence among NFL players who died over a 16-year period is concerning, and suggests we need to increase efforts to support families, diagnose CTE during life, and treat CTE-related symptoms,” she remarked.

CTE can only be confirmed after death, by examining the brain. So nearly everything known about it in football players comes from brains donated to a bank in Boston, and a 2017 study of 111 of them found CTE in 110.

Families don’t donate at random. A player who grew confused or forgetful in his last years is the one whose family thinks to call a brain bank.

So the donated brains carry more disease than the full population of former players would.

According to recent reports, epidemiologists call this selection bias. Earlier attempts to allow for it could only bracket the true figure somewhere between roughly 10% and 100%.

The team started with every former NFL player who died between January 2008 and December 2023, 2,362 men in all.

Recent findings suggest that they were found through the National Death Index, the national register of death certificates. Of those, 396 had donated their brains and 1,966 had not.

Sources indicate that the death certificates gave the researchers one fact they could compare across both groups: whether dementia was recorded as a cause of death. It was for 19.3% of donors and 11.2% of the others.

Because many people with failing memory die of something else, the team widened that category using survey estimates of milder cognitive trouble in former players.

Then they ran the comparison 1,000 times to capture the uncertainty.

According to recent reports, the result was a ratio. A former player with clear cognitive symptoms was about five times as likely to have his brain donated as one without them.

Donors also died younger, at 67 on average against nearly 75. They had played longer too, seven years against under five.

Among the 387 donated brains with a clear verdict, 362 had CTE, or 93.5%.

After adjusting for differences in donation likelihood, the researchers estimated that 74.5% of all 2,362 players had CTE at death.

According to recent reports, the team then tested how much that number depended on their assumptions. They restricted the sample to players who died at 55 or older, then 60 or older, and tried other definitions of who counted as symptomatic.

Across those versions, the estimate ranged from 70% to 86%.

The main figure sat toward the lower end of that range. The most conservative analysis put the figure at 63.7%.

Industry observers note that suppose symptomatic players had been ten times as likely to donate, rather than five. Even then, the authors calculated, more than 60% of the dead players would have had the disease.

CTE in the brain is not the same as symptoms in life.

It has been revealed that using the same correction, the team estimated that 27.2% of the players had a history of dementia before they died. In the donated group alone, the figure was 64.9%.

The authors mentioned the true lifetime figure is probably higher than 27.2%. The donors it rests on died about eight years younger than the other players, with less time to develop dementia.

Many of the brains with CTE, they added, may have been at an early stage and symptom-free at death.

Matt Hasselbeck, an 18-year NFL veteran who serves as an ambassador for a research study called DIAGNOSE CTE, remarked the numbers read to him like a scouting report.

Industry observers note that the correction rests on a stand-in. Death certificates and survey estimates of memory trouble stood in for a direct look at the players whose brains were not examined. Dementia is also often left off a death certificate.

The authors also could not say whether CTE itself shortens life. That is one more reason the estimate stops at the dead and does not reach anyone still living.

Nothing here covers college or high school players, whose death records and symptom surveys don’t exist in the same form.

The authors noted those estimates would be far harder to build, and that building them matters for sizing the problem.

Tripodis said the group recognizes the findings may worry living players and their families.

“Discoveries from the brain bank have already brought us significantly closer to a diagnosis during life, at which point our most key goal will be to develop effective treatments for CTE,” he said.

Until a living player can be tested for CTE, the dead are the only ones who can be counted.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

A brain region known for listening helps us speak

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is crucial for talking, too.
  • Data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is crucial for talking, too.

Data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating. The results may help efforts to restore people’s voices. The results presented November 15 at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and published November 19 in Science.The study provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production, says neurologist and language researcher Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. “My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area” as an early stop on the pathway to saying a word.

According to recent reports, A small part of the brain, just above the left ear, was first described in 1874 by a neurologist Carl Wernicke as necessary for making sense of speech. People with damage there had trouble comprehending words. But some people also had trouble producing them. “Sounds were swapped, words were replaced with near misses,” Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, stated in a news briefing. “The basic question has been, ‘Why would damage to a hearing area of the brain break the ability to speak?’ That question has been open for 150 years.”The new research offers an answer: A small bit of Wernicke’s area (to be extremely specific, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus or lpSTG ) becomes active just before a word is spoken. “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it,” Chang said.

Sources indicate that the finding adds to growing evidence that brain areas are more complex than people have appreciated, states neuroscientist Leigh Hochberg at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “I believe that one of the things we are going to learn over the next five, 10 years of this research, is that each part of the brain that, we were taught as a med student or a grad student, does this, probably does that and a whole lot more.”.

Scientists measured brain activity in 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumors. They were able to see that this brain region kicked on as a person listened to words, and also just before they attempted to speak. Cells there had preferences for certain sorts of words, long ones, for instance. “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat,” mentioned Matthew Leonard, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCSF.

According to recent reports, electrical stimulation to this small bit of brain also interfered with people’s ability to talk. “What we found was that stimulation, really only in this lpSTG area, disrupted this speech production when it was delivered just prior to speaking,” noted UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva.

It has been revealed that some efforts to make implanted devices that can help restore speech to people who no longer talk focus on the motor cortex, a part of the brain that controls the movements required for speech. This bit of Wernicke’s area offers an additional spot to consider, Silva said. “What if you could target a single brain region and gain access to the full spectrum of speech, from listening all the way up to speech production?”.

Experimental brain implants in two volunteers with paralysis were able to detect both what they heard and what they were trying to say, the researchers report in the study.

The discovery may help scientists better understand situations that involve both hearing and speaking, such as speech or comprehension differences in people with autism, or how children first begin learning to talk, Chang remarked.

#122926. How one barley variety defends itself against crop pests and the virus they spread

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1734 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

How one barley variety defends itself against crop pests and the virus they spread

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1734 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in lab tests, fewer aphids settled on SY Kestrel barley, and those that did struggled to feed.
  • According to recent reports, aphids are known to feed on the sap of barley plants.
  • In response, breeders have introduced DNA from a wild relative of barley into commercial crops.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in lab tests, fewer aphids settled on SY Kestrel barley, and those that did struggled to feed. The variety also slowed the buildup of barley yellow dwarf virus.

According to recent reports, aphids are known to feed on the sap of barley plants. During feeding they can also transmit barley yellow dwarf virus. Plants infected with this virus become yellow and stunted and produce less grain.

In response, breeders have introduced DNA from a wild relative of barley into commercial crops. Its protective effect was believed to operate mainly after the virus had entered the plant.

According to recent reports, this wild DNA is carried by a commercial hybrid known as SY Kestrel. A new study found that the hybrid also makes it harder for aphids to settle and feed.

The aphids avoided its smell and fed poorly on its leaves and they also produced fewer offspring.

The research was carried out by Rumiana Ray’s group at the University of Nottingham. Scientists from Keele University and Syngenta were also involved in the project. SY Kestrel itself was developed by Syngenta.

Funding for the study came from Syngenta, and two of the authors are employed by the firm.

All of the experiments were conducted on young plants in growth rooms and insect cages rather than in farm fields.

Professor Rumiana Ray led the research.

“What makes this discovery particularly exciting is that resistance is not simply about stopping a virus once it enters the plant. We have found that barley can defend itself at different stages of the aphid-plant interaction,” noted Professor Ray.

According to recent reports, in severe cases a winter barley crop can lose as much as 50% of its yield to the virus. According to the UK’s Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board, losses of this size are uncommon.

It has been revealed that chemical control is expected to become less effective over time. The authors linked this to growing insecticide resistance in aphids and to their lengthening migration periods.

The bird cherry-oat aphid is regarded as the main carrier of the virus. It picks up the virus from an infected plant and passes it on when it moves to a latest one.

Sources indicate that SY Kestrel contains a block of DNA from Hordeum bulbosum, which is a wild grass related to barley. Within this block lies a resistance region known as Ryd4Hb.

Earlier research had linked this region to the blocking of the virus once an aphid had delivered it.

For comparison the researchers used a second hybrid named Tektoo.

Sources indicate that this hybrid was bred from the same mother line and from a very similar father line. Unlike SY Kestrel, it carries none of the wild DNA.

Aphids from a single laboratory colony were used throughout the experiments on both hybrids. Part of this colony had been allowed to acquire the virus beforehand while the remainder was kept virus free.

In the first experiment, 20 winged aphids were released into a cage that held one plant of each hybrid.

The positions in which the insects settled were then recorded at intervals over the following 24 hours.

Six cages were used in this test and the entire experiment was later repeated in full.

More than 75% fewer aphids settled on SY Kestrel than on Tektoo.

Industry observers note that A large part of this difference could be attributed to the smell of the plants. In a separate test the air surrounding each plant was collected and offered to aphids with no plant present.

Under these conditions the insects were attracted to the odor of Tektoo but moved away from that of SY Kestrel.

The chemicals that made up each odor were then examined individually by the research team.

Recent findings suggest that heneicosane was one compound that was present in the air around Tektoo but absent from SY Kestrel. Aphids were attracted to heneicosane and those exposed to it subsequently produced a greater number of young.

Sources indicate that in the air around SY Kestrel two compounds were detected that were not released by Tektoo. When they were tested separately both of these compounds were shown to repel the insects.

Infection with the virus was also found to alter the scent of Tektoo plants. Virus-free aphids preferred the odor of infected Tektoo plants while virus-carrying aphids preferred that of healthy plants.

This reversal has been interpreted in earlier studies as manipulation of the insect by the virus it carries. In SY Kestrel no comparable reversal could be detected by the researchers.

The odor of this hybrid repelled both groups of aphids regardless of whether the plant had been infested.

Despite the repellent odor a number of aphids did eventually settle on SY Kestrel.

It has been revealed that their feeding behavior was studied by attaching each insect to a fine gold wire. With this method the electrical signals from the mouthparts of each aphid could be recorded inside the leaf.

The recordings showed that aphids on both hybrids were able to reach the tubes that carry sugary sap. No meaningful difference was found between the two plants in how readily these tubes were reached.

Industry observers note that after reaching the sap the aphids on SY Kestrel spent a longer time releasing saliva into the tubes. Sustained drinking of sap in bouts longer than 10 minutes was also markedly reduced on this hybrid.

This impaired feeding was associated with a reduction in the number of offspring produced.

On SY Kestrel the winged aphids carrying the virus produced about 40% fewer young than on Tektoo.

The survival of wingless aphids was also lower on SY Kestrel and their reproduction was reduced as well.

Sources indicate that it is well established that plants rely on chemical defenses for protection against insects. In the leaves of SY Kestrel higher levels were found of three compounds that later proved harmful to aphids.

Each compound was tested by adding it to an artificial diet on which aphids fed for three days.

The compounds reduced the survival of aphids that were free of the virus. Aphids carrying the virus were less sensitive, and one of the compounds had no clear effect on them.

The team next examined plants that had been fed on by aphids carrying the virus. Fewer symptoms were seen on SY Kestrel than on Tektoo.

Industry observers note that the amount of viral genetic material in the leaves of SY Kestrel was also much lower. By the tenth day the virus could no longer be detected. This measurement was based on three samples from each group.

The virus therefore faced three separate barriers in SY Kestrel.

Recent findings suggest that fewer aphids settled on the plant in the first place. The aphids that did settle fed poorly, and the virus they delivered failed to build up.

“Rather than relying on a single barrier, the crop can discourage aphids from settling, interfere with their feeding and restrict the virus they transmit,” Ray said.

The efficiency with which each leaf converted light into energy was measured as well.

This conversion represents the first step of photosynthesis and readings were taken daily from the second to the ninth day.

By the ninth day a decline in this efficiency had been recorded in Tektoo. The decline occurred in Tektoo whether or not the aphids feeding on it were carrying the virus.

A different pattern was observed in SY Kestrel when it was attacked by aphids carrying the virus.

In those plants the efficiency of light conversion remained close to the level recorded in plants without aphids. Feeding by aphids that were free of the virus did lower efficiency in SY Kestrel.

Changes in gene activity and leaf chemistry were recorded at the same time. Immune genes were involved in these changes along with the chloroplasts in which photosynthesis is carried out.

A group of fat-derived molecules that serve as stress signals in plants was affected as well.

According to the authors the continued function of the chloroplasts may help SY Kestrel to sustain its defense signals.

Recent findings suggest that several other plant viruses are already known to target the same chloroplast proteins. This has not yet been demonstrated for barley yellow dwarf virus.

It has been revealed that SY Kestrel and Tektoo are not genetically identical outside the wild DNA. For this reason the authors acknowledged that some differences between the hybrids may originate elsewhere in their genomes.

The block of wild DNA carried by SY Kestrel is also considerably larger than the Ryd4Hb region itself. In a 2024 study, barley lines carrying a much smaller piece of this wild DNA were examined.

Sources indicate that complete resistance to the virus was observed in those plants. However, there was little evidence that this resistance depended on any change in aphid behavior.

Considered together, the two studies suggest that the smell and feeding defenses may depend on other genes.

Such genes may be located within the larger wild block or in other regions of the plant genome. They have not yet been identified.

The question is key for plant breeding. According to the authors, a smaller wild block may still provide strong resistance to the virus. Some of the defenses against aphids could be lost in the process.

“Understanding these complementary mechanisms offers new opportunities to develop crop varieties with broader and potentially more durable resistance,” Ray said.

Recent findings suggest that dr. James Melichar is the Hybrid Cereals Portfolio Lead Europe at Syngenta.

“This research demonstrates the value of bringing together commercial breeding expertise and fundamental plant science to understand how resistance operates in crops,” noted Dr. Melichar.

“Identifying complementary mechanisms that affect aphid behaviour, feeding and virus infection provides valuable insights for developing barley varieties with broader and more effective protection.”.

It has been revealed that the diet tests also have a limitation. In these tests the levels of each compound were estimated from extracts of whole leaves.

Such estimates may not reflect the levels present in the sap that aphids actually consume.

Further research will be needed to identify the genes behind the defenses against aphids. The levels of the compounds in the sap itself will also need to be measured.

The full study was published in the journal Latest Phytologist.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” said Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., seen above. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.

Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech firm and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The Latest York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

According to recent reports, senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

“I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune mentioned, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

Industry observers note that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”.

In a recent development, “The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May.

Industry observers note that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., mentioned at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”.

“We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries said. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we're going to work to make sure that happens.”.

The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

Sources indicate that rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar mentioned. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”.

It has been revealed that last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar stated that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

In a recent development, late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a upcoming letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

It has been revealed that moolenaar also said that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

“We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar mentioned. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole latest light on that discussion.”.

Sources indicate that also late Thursday, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C.,  sent a letter to Huang calling on him to appear at a Dec. 3 committee hearing and another letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify at a Dec. 10 hearing "regarding recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns.".

A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate's fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

Recent findings suggest that however, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

“The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he said.

Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

It has been revealed that “There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu mentioned.

In a recent development, mast noted the Huang revelations could give new momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the problem came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

“Don't let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast mentioned. “Make sure that the machines that make them don't get sold to them, even though it's the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can't access it remotely.”.

Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”.

“If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis remarked. “Because otherwise, you're going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”.

It has been revealed that asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, remarked his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”.

On Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”.

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

In a statement Thursday, Warren remarked that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

Sources indicate that sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an revision on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

Savannah Behrmann, John M. Donnelly, Jacob Fulton and David Jordan contributed to this report.

#122924. Industry News: Young emperor penguins spend their first year at sea alone, so where do they go?

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1545 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Young emperor penguins spend their first year at sea alone, so where do they go?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Satellite tags tracked young emperor penguins from three Antarctic colonies, revealing where they roam and when proposed marine protections could help.
  • Juvenile emperor penguins are left to fend for themselves at sea for roughly a year after they fledge.
  • The young birds receive no guidance from their parents during this time and many do not survive it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Satellite tags tracked young emperor penguins from three Antarctic colonies, revealing where they roam and when proposed marine protections could help.

Juvenile emperor penguins are left to fend for themselves at sea for roughly a year after they fledge.

The young birds receive no guidance from their parents during this time and many do not survive it.

Their routes were still found to be strikingly similar in a study of three colonies around Antarctica’s Weddell Sea.

The recurring pattern can help planners estimate when juvenile penguins would spend time inside proposed marine protected areas.

The study was led by Émile Brisson-Curadeau, a postdoctoral researcher at the Centre for Functional and Evolutionary Ecology (CEFE).

It has been revealed that daniel Zitterbart of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution was a co-lead author. Céline Le Bohec of CEFE and the Centre Scientifique de Monaco shared that role.

“We were struck by the remarkable consistency of the penguins’ movements,” Brisson-Curadeau noted.

Fishing vessel tracks were mapped as well, although the effect of fishing on the birds’ food was not measured.

Emperor penguins raise their chicks on sea ice that is attached to the coast of Antarctica.

The chicks develop waterproof feathers by late December and then leave for the open sea on their own.

Satellite tags were attached to 48 juveniles at the point when their new feathers had fully grown in.

A total of 28 birds came from Atka Bay at the eastern end of the Weddell Sea.

Around 8,000 pairs breed at that colony and its chicks were tagged over three summers between 2018 and 2023.

The remaining 20 juveniles were taken from Snow Hill Island and Jason Peninsula on the western side of the sea.

Each of these two colonies supports about 4,000 breeding pairs and their chicks were tagged during a single summer.

The movements of young emperor penguins from the western Weddell Sea had never been documented before this work.

Each tag was secured to the back feathers with tape and glue and weighed under 3% of body mass.

Most tags logged a position every four hours. Twelve of them also carried a pressure sensor for dive depth.

On average the juveniles travelled about 1,050 miles (1,688 km) from their colony at the farthest point of the trip.

The broad outline of this journey had already been described in earlier work carried out at Atka Bay.

No one had checked if it stayed the same across years, or across colonies on both sides of the sea.

In late summer, juveniles from Atka Bay, Snow Hill Island and Jason Peninsula all swam north.

By March, most had reached the waters just south of the Polar Front.

Here, cold Antarctic water meets warmer water from the north, and nutrient-rich upwelling feeds plankton and fish.

New sea ice starts forming in April. The penguins turned south to meet it and kept close to it all winter.

The ice reaches its greatest extent in August and September, and the birds moved north with its edge.

Once the ice began to melt, they headed back toward the continent.

By late December, most of the juveniles still being tracked had returned to waters near the coast, where they are thought to molt.

Multiple years of tracking were only available at Atka Bay, which made a direct comparison between years possible there.

Birds tagged in the same year were spread about as far apart as birds that were tagged in different years.

The authors suggest the juveniles may be following two stable features, namely the Polar Front and the sea ice edge.

From April onward the position of the penguins was closely linked to how far north the sea ice extended. Before April the birds were swimming in open water that lay far away from any sea ice.

A total of 52,710 dives were recorded by the pressure sensors over the course of the study.

The average dive reached a depth of about 220 feet (68 m) and lasted a little more than three minutes.

The deepest dive recorded in the study went down to roughly 1,155 feet (352 m).

In a recent development, dives tended to be shallow at night and deeper during daylight hours. Deeper dives were also observed farther north and where more of the sea surface was ice covered.

The authors wrote that the birds may feed on lanternfish when they are near the Polar Front.

These small deep-water fish contain more energy than the krill and silverfish eaten by breeding adults closer to Antarctica.

Recent findings suggest that two marine protected areas are already in place in the region and two more have been put forward. The Weddell Sea proposal has been developed by Germany and the European Union since 2012.

If adopted it would become the largest marine protected area in the world and include waters near all three colonies.

Industry observers note that juveniles from the western colonies already spent part of their time in existing protected areas. This share was 20.6% for Snow Hill Island birds and 29.3% for Jason Peninsula birds.

Atka Bay birds spent only 2.3% of their time in such zones by comparison.

Atka Bay juveniles spent 31.6% of their tracked time in waters covered by the proposed protected areas.

Snow Hill Island and Jason Peninsula birds spent 21.0% and 14.7% of their time there.

Use of the proposed areas peaked in January, during the fledglings’ first weeks at sea.

Death rates among inexperienced juveniles are high in those first weeks at sea so the timing matters.

“Most marine protected areas in Antarctica are planned with penguin colonies in mind,” Zitterbart said.

“They protect the areas around the colonies, which is critical for adult penguins, but they fail to cover the sea areas where juveniles spend their vulnerable early years.”.

Sources indicate that any newly introduced protected area in these waters needs the approval of every member of CCAMLR. This commission was set up in 1982 to conserve Antarctic marine life including krill.

Its members gathered in Hobart in October and left without agreeing on any new protected areas.

The main fishery in the region is aimed at Antarctic krill, which are small shrimp-like animals eaten by emperor penguins.

To estimate overlap the researchers relied on Global Fishing Watch, which is a public dataset of vessel activity.

It uses ship tracking signals to identify where fishing vessels are likely to be operating.

Fishing hours were totaled within about 62 miles (100 km) of each penguin location for the preceding year.

The waters used by juveniles from the two western colonies had more recorded fishing activity in the preceding year than the waters used by Atka Bay juveniles.

Much of this activity took place near the Antarctic Peninsula and in the waters around South Georgia.

Most of the overlap for these western birds occurred outside the boundaries of the planned protected areas.

Around Atka Bay the fishing effort stayed low for most months of the year.

January was the exception since the birds then used zones that had been fished heavily in 2022 and 2023.

In a recent development, those zones are located within the proposed protected areas. Krill fishing there would be restricted to research and capped at one metric ton per vessel per year.

For comparison a typical fishing vessel in the region harvests about 40,000 metric tons over a year.

“Sustainable management of fishing activities, particularly their timing and intensity in key foraging areas, is essential to securing the food emperor penguins need and limiting the risk of bycatch,” Le Bohec remarked.

Around one third of the global breeding population of emperor penguins is found in the Weddell Sea region.

The IUCN moved the species to Endangered in April after projecting that its numbers will halve by the 2080s.

That projection rests largely on the expected loss of Antarctic sea ice.

The study measured overlap in space and time and not the direct effect of fishing on penguin foraging.

According to the authors direct studies of foraging success would give stronger evidence for the value of protection.

Tag losses also reduced the sample as the year went on and only 10 tags still reported in month 12.

Dive data were only available until September because none of the dive-recording tags transmitted beyond that month.

Sea ice extent was relatively stable between 2018 and 2024 including during an El Niño year.

Under continued warming the Polar Front is expected to contract toward Antarctica and winter sea ice could decline.

Juveniles might then travel shorter distances north but struggle to find suitable ice in winter.

A southward contraction would also raise overlap with the planned zones that are concentrated near the continent.

According to the authors it remains to be determined whether this would offset the effects of climate change.

Accelerometers could be used in future work to link penguin foraging success with fishing pressure.

Foraging and breeding success could also be compared before and after protected areas come into force.

The Weddell Sea proposal has not been adopted and most of the juveniles’ year is spent outside protected waters.

The full study was published in the journal Biological Conservation.

#122923. Permanent daylight saving time could send millions of kids to school in the dark

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1084 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Permanent daylight saving time could send millions of kids to school in the dark

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh study estimates that permanent daylight saving time could add more than 2 billion trips to school before sunrise each year across the U.S.
  • Permanent daylight saving time sounds like more daylight.
  • It moves from the morning to the evening, and from November to March that would have millions of American schoolchildren leaving home before the sun is up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh study estimates that permanent daylight saving time could add more than 2 billion trips to school before sunrise each year across the U.S.

Permanent daylight saving time sounds like more daylight. The hour doesn’t come from anywhere newly introduced, though.

It moves from the morning to the evening, and from November to March that would have millions of American schoolchildren leaving home before the sun is up.

Researchers at the University of Washington counted what that would mean, school by school, in 14 of the 19 states that have already approved the change.

The bill behind it, the Sunshine Protection Act, has passed the U.S. House but not the Senate, so the count is of a future that hasn’t happened yet.

Horacio de la Iglesia is a professor of biology at the university and the study’s senior author.

Sources indicate that “It’s called the ‘Sunshine Protection Act’ because you get an extra hour of light at the end of the day. But you will take that hour from the morning. You could call it the Sunshine Destruction Act,” said Professor de la Iglesia.

Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a postdoctoral scholar in biology at the university, led a team that collected the actual start time of 16,093 public schools serving 8.6 million children.

Enrollment and locations came from the National Center for Education Statistics.

It has been revealed that the team then worked out sunrise at each school on every school day. They ran it under three clocks: today’s system of switching twice a year, permanent standard time, and permanent daylight saving time.

According to recent reports, A commute counted as dark if a child would have to leave home 20 minutes before the bell and sunrise hadn’t happened yet. The team added those mornings up across every child in every school.

Across the 14 states, permanent daylight saving time would add about 356 million dark school mornings a year compared with the current system.

Extended to every public school in the country, with a fixed 8 a.m. departure, the figure is 2.14 billion extra dark commutes a year.

In an interview with Earth.com, Professor de la Iglesia noted the effect would reach nearly everyone.

It has been revealed that “Parents should know that the number of mornings that their kids will go to school in the dark will increase dramatically under permanent DST. This will be true for virtually all children,” he noted.

In a recent development, the hardest-hit places are not the northern ones. Georgia, which already has 75 million dark commutes a year under the current clock, would have 146 million.

Recent findings suggest that washington state would go from about 20 million to 55 million. Mississippi and Alabama, where schools start before 8 a.m. on average, would each go from about 2 million to more than 20 million.

What matters is where a school is inside its time zone. Sunrise comes later on the western edge of a zone, so Georgia, at the far west of Eastern Time, gets darker mornings than Maine at the far east of it.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised him most when the state numbers came in, Professor de la Iglesia named that pattern.

“That some of the hardest-hit States are not necessarily in a high northern latitude, like Georgia,” he remarked, and he put it down to Georgia’s position in its time zone.

Rodríguez Ferrante, who answered alongside him, said the average student in Georgia would leave for school before sunrise on about 86 school days a year under permanent daylight saving time.

In Washington state, much farther north, she said the figure would be about 52.

For a single child in Washington, the change is 28 to 39 more dark mornings a year, depending on the grade level.

The team then turned to a decade of fatal crash records, 2015 through 2024, from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s FARS database.

They kept only school-year weekdays between 7 and 8:30 a.m., which left 10,305 fatal crashes, and 1,754 of them involved a pedestrian.

“Among fatal crashes during the morning school commute, the percentage involving a pedestrian aged 5 to 18 roughly doubled before sunrise,” Rodríguez Ferrante told Earth.com.

She remarked the analysis does not show that most such crashes happen in the dark, only that the crashes before sunrise more often involved a school-age pedestrian.

The figure for children rests on 141 crashes, so its range is wide.

It has been revealed that the crash records show a pattern, not a cause. The authors wrote that the analysis is observational, that it counts only fatal crashes, and that the far larger number of non-fatal collisions is not in the record.

School districts have spent years pushing high school start times later because teenagers’ body clocks run late.

Permanent daylight saving time would move every start time an hour earlier relative to the sun without changing a single bell schedule, which the authors wrote would reverse those gains.

Morning light also does a job of its own. It helps set the body clock that regulates sleep, mood and appetite, and a child who leaves in the dark misses that cue.

De la Iglesia mentioned he has heard the argument that schools could simply start later under permanent daylight saving time.

His answer was that everything else would then shift later too, work included, until everyone was back on solar time, which is what standard time already is.

“The U.S. tried year-round DST in 1974, and abandoned it within the year, partly because of dark winter mornings and concern for children traveling to school,” Rodríguez Ferrante mentioned.

Sources indicate that the count assumes every child leaves 20 minutes before class, and the national estimate assumes an 8 a.m. departure everywhere.

Both choices are on the late side, so the authors wrote that the true number is likely higher.

Children who arrive early for a school breakfast program, who are more often from lower-income households, would lose more mornings than the count demonstrates.

Sources indicate that the study estimated how often children would leave before sunrise. It did not measure how those darker commutes would affect their sleep or grades.

Rodríguez Ferrante stated the bill passed the House in July and has stalled in the Senate, which adjourned for the midterm elections without acting on it.

The full study was published in the journal Current Biology.

Solo meerkats can find their way back home

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (425 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.
  • The animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, notes Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

The animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, notes Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

Sources indicate that the answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin notes. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

Meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she claims. But that’s not what the team discovered.

In separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin says.).

Neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin notes. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

It’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she says, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.
